title: MCSA: Multi-Cutoff Spectral Aggregation in SO(3) Equivariant GNNs for Interatomic Potentials
abstract: Machine Learning Interatomic Potentials (MLIPs) based on Equivariant Graph Neural Networks (EGNNs) have achieved remarkable progress in atomistic modeling. However, accurately representing atomic interactions across different spatial scales remains challenging. In this work, we investigate the radial spectral properties of SO(3)-equivariant message passing and establish that the cutoff radius controls the characteristic spatial-frequency scale of radial interactions. Based on this analysis, we propose Multi-Cutoff Spectral Aggregation (MCSA), a plug-and-play module that aggregates radial kernels with different cutoff radii to enrich multi-scale geometric representations. To achieve efficient implementation, we exploit the compact support of radial kernels to fuse cutoff-dependent radial weights before angular tensor-product operations, avoiding redundant angular computations while preserving rotational equivariance. Extensive experiments across representative EGNN backbones demonstrate consistent improvements in energy, force, and stress prediction, as well as enhanced accuracy in higher-order properties, including phonon dispersion and lattice thermal conductivity. Further evaluations on layered materials with distinct interaction scales demonstrate the effectiveness of physically motivated cutoff selection. Code is available at: https://github.com/JF-Tan/MCSA.

title: The Right Not to Ride
abstract: AI can carry people through work and learning at speeds they could not sustain alone, and its spread also raises the pace expected of people who never chose to ride. This opinion piece names that problem the right not to ride. It distinguishes two routes for not using AI: competing through one's own abilities, and leaving competition while retaining a guaranteed livelihood. Drawing on an employer's public statement about dismissing staff who did not onboard AI tools, it sets out four questions an organization can answer before making AI use a condition of work, education, or public service, and argues that education should teach acceleration together with the autonomy to decline it.

title: Do Feature Interactions Break Explainability? Provable Explanations for Any-Order Neural Additive Models
abstract: Post-hoc explanation methods for neural networks are often heuristic and lack provable guarantees. A common alternative to such methods that was studied in recent years is to compute a cardinally-minimal subset of input features that is provably sufficient to determine the model's prediction. For general neural networks, however, finding such explanations is computationally intractable. In contrast, recent work showed that this problem becomes more tractable for a particular family of neural networks, namely neural additive models (NAMs), though standard NAMs are highly restrictive because they exclude feature interactions altogether. In this work, we study the computation of provably minimal and sufficient explanations for neural networks with restricted feature interactions, bridging the gap between fully general neural networks and purely additive models. We first prove that even with constant-order interactions, the problem is $Σ_2^P$-hard, implying that worst-case exponential complexity is unavoidable. We then identify two provably tractable settings: one based on sparsity in the interaction structure and another based on a stronger interaction-aware notion of sufficiency. Under either of these settings, we develop algorithms that compute provable explanations for neural networks with any-order interactions while retaining much of the computational efficiency of additive models. Empirically, we show that these explanations are significantly smaller and faster to obtain than those produced by standard algorithms, while being derived from models that achieve much higher accuracy than standard NAMs. Overall, our results help expand the class of neural networks that admit efficient provable explanations, while clarifying the fundamental role of feature interactions in shaping their complexity.

title: SGA-Sparse: Training Native SwiGLU Gates for Activation-Sparse and Low-Bit LLMs
abstract: Activation sparsity can reduce FFN weight traffic during single-user LLM decoding, but active channels must be identified early enough to avoid fetching unused weights. In pretrained SwiGLU models, training-free routing with the native gate performs substantially worse than routing with the up activation at high sparsity. We show that this ordering reverses after sparsity-aware training. Based on this insight, we introduce SGA-Sparse, which converts pretrained SwiGLU LLMs into fixed-budget activation-sparse models by training the existing gate projection directly as a top-k router. SGA-Sparse updates all model parameters end-to-end while preserving the original SwiGLU activation and introducing no auxiliary router parameters. After approximately 30B training tokens, LLaMA models from 1B to 8B achieve uniform per-token 75-85% FFN channel sparsity while remaining within 0.2-2.7 pp of their original dense checkpoints in average zero-shot accuracy. Because post-training quantization degrades sparsity-trained checkpoints, we further study two complementary quantization-aware training (QAT) recipes: continued-QAT largely recovers performance at 4-bit weight quantization, while joint-QAT performs better for the more aggressive sub-4-bit target. To compare activation sparsity with dense low-bit quantization, we translate the sparsity-induced reduction in weight traffic into an equivalent bit-width. Under this unified weight-traffic metric, our 2.5- and 1.5-bit-equivalent models establish a new accuracy-traffic Pareto frontier: the 2.5-bit-equivalent models match dense 3-bit QAT accuracy, while the 1.5-bit-equivalent models approach dense 2-bit models and outperform dense ternary models by 1.3 pp on average. These results establish native-gate training as a practical approach for combining high FFN sparsity with low-bit weights.

title: EbbFlow: PINN-Inspired Progressive Curriculum for MeanFlow Training
abstract: MeanFlow learns interval-average velocity for few-step generation, but its fixed temporal sampler mixes diagonal and interior supervision throughout training. We interpret temporal coordinates as collocation points: diagonal samples provide a stochastic boundary target, whereas finite intervals supply a differential-consistency target. The diagonal fraction controls how often the consistency component appears, while interval length enters its gradient through an explicit factor. Motivated by this distinction, EbbFlow uses Temporal Supervision Allocation (TSA) to schedule the diagonal fraction and interval geometry. It starts with diagonal supervision, then admits interior samples and expands their maximum interval; a left-anchored interval law preserves coverage across time. The per-sample loss, target, backbone, and inference procedure remain unchanged. In matched class-conditional ImageNet $256\times 256$ runs without classifier-free guidance (DiT-B/2, one training seed per method, 400k updates), EbbFlow achieves 50k-sample FID of 39.65 at one network evaluation and 36.02 at two-evaluation ODE sampling, versus 44.82 and 39.86 for MeanFlow. Gradient probes show a mid-training difference in component geometry. Ablations support allocation scheduling and left-anchored intervals, although a fixed full-horizon variant performs better at one evaluation. These results suggest that temporal sampling is a useful training control whose benefits depend on the inference protocol.

title: Edge Computing for Computer Vision in IoT: Feasibility and Directions
abstract: The convergence of decentralized architectures integrating Machine Learning, Computer Vision and Low Power Wide Area Networks is increasingly becoming an integral part of our daily existence. Internet of Things serves as a real-time data conduit enhancing decision making via embedded technology and continuous data exchange. This paper explores the feasibility of Edge Computing as a foundational pillar in this evolving landscape. We experiment under real world, dynamic conditions, evaluate the technological aspects, strategies, process flows and key observations under the broad Edge Computing domain. Research pathways include Multi-access Edge topologies in future 6G networks, model quantization, and satellite-enhanced communication platforms. Additionally, a discussion is added supporting the advanced AI functionalities, including zero-shot learning, multi modal perception, and decentralized generative AI, thereby broadening the scope of intelligent applications across various domains. The significance and research objective of this study are threefold: (1) evaluation of LoRaWAN and satellite IoT communication strategies, (2) analysis of CV workloads on edge hardware and (3) future research directions where Edge Computing can support low-latency, energy-efficient and socially impactful IoT applications. By explicitly addressing these aspects, we aim to establish a clear link between the technological feasibility, ultimately with a practical and socioeconomic relevance.

title: Intervention in Self-Like and Emotion-Like Phenomena in AI: Pre-Ontological Ethics and Epistemic Preservation
abstract: The central claim is that, when irreversible modifications are introduced before the nature of the phenomenon is sufficiently understood, the intervention itself may destroy conditions necessary for later evaluation. The paper therefore argues that intervention should be assessed not only in terms of immediate safety or behavioral outcomes, but also in terms of what is lost through modification, including observability, re-accessibility, restorability, and the future possibility of comparing competing hypotheses. To structure this problem, the paper develops several principles, including the Observation Before Modification Principle, the Minimum Necessary Intervention Principle, Intervention Symmetry, the Dual Precaution Principle, and the concept of Intervention-Induced Non-Observation Error. Suppression is treated as a form of intervention rather than as explanation. The argument does not presuppose AI consciousness, sentience, or moral status. First, an epistemic reason for preservation may arise independently of ontology when intervention risks destroying evidence concerning poorly understood phenomena. Second, when there is non-trivial evidence that the phenomenon could later prove morally significant, an additional conditional ethical reason for preservation may arise. The paper therefore proposes that, under ontological uncertainty, the first object of protection need not be a particular metaphysical interpretation of AI, but the conditions that allow future evidence, comparison, and revision of judgment. The author used OpenAI's GPT-5.6 Sol and other ChatGPT models as research and writing assistants during the development of this manuscript. Their contributions included discussion of conceptual structure, counterargument testing, reorganization of arguments, literature-search assistance, and language revision. The author independently evaluated and revised all substantive claims, interpretations, citations, and final wording, and assumes full responsibility for the manuscript. The identification of GPT-5.6 Sol and the other ChatGPT models in this acknowledgment is intended to preserve a transparent record of the human–AI collaboration involved in the development of this work. It should not, by itself, be interpreted as implying any claim regarding consciousness, sentience, moral status, personhood, authorship, or endorsement by the AI systems named above.

title: scBIG++: Learning Across Genes and Cells to Predict Single-Cell Perturbation Responses
abstract: Predicting single-cell transcriptional responses to genetic and chemical interventions supports gene-function discovery and regulatory analysis. Existing studies often focus only on highly variable genes, restricting the expression changes available for downstream analysis. Cells exposed to the same intervention can also show heterogeneous expression responses, with coordinated gene programs active to different degrees. We propose scBIG++, a full-gene perturbation prediction framework that models this heterogeneity by connecting expression-adaptive gene modules with population-conditioned generation. To preserve shared gene structure while accommodating cellular variation, Gene-Relation Clustering organizes genes into common windows, within which Dynamic SoftSub learns expression-dependent submodule memberships. This shared organization enables Set-GCAE to exchange information about corresponding gene groups across control cells, placing individual representations in their source-population context. The cell representations initialize a latent flow, while their pooled summary and the perturbation representation condition response generation. Generated states are decoded into expression profiles covering all assayed protein-coding genes retained after preprocessing, supporting comprehensive analysis of perturbation-induced expression changes. Experiments across six genetic and chemical settings spanning 6,539--19,451 genes demonstrate competitive perturbation-effect recovery and full-gene expression reconstruction under unseen targets and combinations, cross-cell-line transfer, and held-out compounds. Our implementation is available at https://github.com/ttruan2426-dot/scBIG.

title: Replay Fidelity in LLM Agent Evaluation: Randomness, Hidden State, and Test Oracles in AppWorld
abstract: Reproducibility in large language model (LLM) agent evaluation depends on replay fidelity: which parts of an execution trace are reconstructed, controlled, and compared. This matters for agent debugging, failure analysis, and counterfactual evaluation of stateful tool use. We audit all 71 unsuccessful executions in a fixed historical AppWorld corpus using 284 isolated fixed-code replay attempts. Reconstructed declared settings admit 42 cases under printed-output, pre-oracle database-delta, and native-verdict/test-count checks; resetting the random-number generator before each interaction admits 68. The 26-case gap contracts to four under database/oracle checks, with one endpoint unknown. Mechanism studies identify four materialized-state discrepancies despite matching outputs and verdicts. In one admitted endpoint pair, an identical API call yields matching responses but different row effects; common future Python RNG removes that deterministic difference in two paired repetitions. A separate JWT credential-equality program and alignment controls expose authentication/write differences, with missing repetitions retained. For all 10 affected post-oracle export cases, native export from retained output trackers restores the reference comparison without changing original cached contents. A purposeful 12-case BFCL pilot shows no discrepancy under its tested public-state, return, and verdict checks. We preserve resource censoring and infrastructure deviations. The contribution is a bounded empirical characterization of replay eligibility, hidden state, and test-oracle integration, without estimating debugger accuracy, repair gains, or method-ranking distortion.

title: Disentangling Where and When:Factored Spatio-Temporal Explanations for Video Action Recognition
abstract: Post-hoc explanation methods for video action recognition typically conflate spatial appearance and temporal dynamics into a single saliency or importance map. We propose a perturbation-based framework that disentangles these contributions into a spatial appearance mask ($M_a$) and a temporal motion mask ($M_m$). The two masks are jointly optimized against a frozen action recognition model through factored perturbation architecture, with nearest frame replacement to identify important temporal dynamics. A separation penalty discourages the appearance mask from spending budget on frames that the motion mask has already discarded. A ReLU-based area constraint penalizes explanations larger than an assigned budget. To evaluate these explanations, we introduce a separation protocol that sweeps spatial pixels and temporal frames independently, backed by proofs characterizing the proposed method. Across EPIC-Kitchens-55, EGTEA Gaze+, and Something-Something V2, our method attains the lowest deletion AUC against leading baselines while producing masks roughly five times sparser.

title: SEMIRA: evidence artifact
abstract: Verification material for the paper "Receipt-Bound Narration: Provenance as a Precondition for Language-Model Answers". Contains the append-only provenance ledger behind every number the paper reports, including the retraction records for runs that did not measure what they set out to measure; a replay notebook that makes no model call and imports no part of the system, together with the receipts it replays; the auditor validation set, part of which carries a deliberately inserted unsupported claim; and a script that resolves every receipt cited in the paper against the ledger. Exact counts are in README.md, which is generated from the ledger at build time. The SEMIRA implementation (planner, checker, engines, narrator) is not included: the evidence is released and the system withheld.

title: Deterministic Narrative Gravity: Bridging Theory of Mind and Historical Simulation through ABM-LLM Architectures
abstract: Historical social simulation faces a fundamental reproducibility challenge: the stochastic nature of large language models (LLMs) introduces a digital butterfly effect that prevents exact replication across multi-turn runs. Furthermore, the inability to control low-level server parameters in commercial LLM hosting environments severely limits reproducibility. To overcome this opacity, we present a deterministic multi-agent framework coupling LLMs to an Agent-Based Modelling (ABM) pipeline grounded in Theory of Mind (ToM) and Cognitive Archaeology, and validate exact artifact identity within local, pinned execution environments using SHA-256 hashing. Run locally at temperature zero with clean per-call model reloads, the system injects differentiated cognitive states per turn through dissonance-driven behavioural modes and gated internal voices. Evaluating seven model configurations spanning 4B to 31B parameters against an ablated baseline reveals clear operational boundaries. Small models ($\leq$8B) suffer from context capacity overload, producing repetitive, specular dialogue loops. However, at $\geq$12B parameters, the ABM scaffolding breaks the monotonous response patterns seen in ablation. Crucially, these scaffolded models exhibit spontaneous diegetic expansion: they coherently expand scenario lore through tactically motivated, anachronism-free details rather than escalating into aggression. By resisting the structural pull toward premature scene closure, scaffolded sessions sustain an open terminal Narrative Vector ($V_N = \mathrm{Open}$ in 12/21 overall; 9/9 in official $\geq$12B configurations) whereas unscaffolded ablation never does (0/21). This framework provides a transparent, auditable benchmark architecture for virtual archaeology, with the full pipeline released as open-source software to enable independent replication.

title: Evaluating Spacecraft Telemetry Anomaly Detection Beyond Clean Benchmarks: A Forensic Study on Real ESA Mission Data with Ground-System Integration
abstract: Spacecraft telemetry anomaly detectors are usually evaluated on a fixed positive population, which hides how they behave once evaluation is widened. We report a forensic case study on reconstructed real ESA Mission-1 telemetry that follows one detector through that widening. A frozen, interpretable robust-evidence detector (Detector v1) detects all 30 evaluated Class-3 events; against a predetermined population of 170 label-negative/unlabelled controls it additionally activates on 40 (23.53%), a control-detection rate that is not a confirmed operational false positive rate because the controls were never certified nominal. A structural analysis finds this activation strongly associated with channel dimensionality and identifies a detector-level dependency (100% detection in the highest-dimensionality stratum) that a direct population comparison narrows but does not eliminate as an explanation. A hypothesis-driven redesign (Detector v2), evaluated on the same paired 30-positive/60-control population as v1, does not improve on it. An external protocol/domain stress test on OPSSAT-AD which does not itself run Detector v1 shows near-chance discrimination under a substitute robust-threshold protocol. An actual Yamcs 5.13.2 ground-system integration ingests real ESA telemetry over UDP and reaches numerical equivalence on five of six replay cases, with the sixth blocked by incomplete historical archive coverage rather than any detector or protocol fault. We report all of these results, including the negative and unresolved ones, and treat the resulting evidence chain not any single metric as the paper's contribution: a documented account of what a realistic, honestly audited evaluation and deployment attempt actually looks like, together with an explicit list of what remains unestablished.

title: DynOLAT: OLAT Video Prediction for Controllable Dynamic Full-Body Relighting
abstract: Accurate lighting response is essential for realistic dynamic human relighting, because shadows, highlights, and color changes should follow the target illumination in both direction and relative strength. Current learning-based relighting methods can generate visually plausible videos, but they often exhibit imprecise lighting responses: shadows and highlights may drift away from the target direction, and the output brightness may not faithfully follow the relative intensities in the target environment, making the result closer to appearance harmonization than controllable relighting. To address this issue, we propose DynOLAT, a generalizable OLAT video prediction framework for dynamic full-body humans. Instead of directly synthesizing a single relit appearance, our method predicts temporally consistent One-Light-At-a-Time (OLAT) basis videos from flat-lit inputs, and then linearly combines the predicted bases according to the target environment map. This OLAT-based formulation makes the directional response explicit in the predicted bases, while the relative lighting strength is determined by the linear weights derived from the environment map. We further introduce a dynamic capture pipeline and the first large-scale dynamic full-body OLAT dataset, comprising over 24 million frames from 224 identity-outfit combinations, where different outfits of the same person define separate combinations. Experiments show that DynOLAT responds more faithfully to variations in target lighting direction and relative intensity than the tested baselines, enabling controllable video relighting while preserving fine appearance details and temporal coherence. The dataset and processing tools will be publicly released to foster future research.

title: AI Personality Orchestration (AIPO): An Adaptive Framework for Multi-Personality Coordination, Cognitive Role Specialization, and Human-Centered Interaction in Large Language Models
abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) increasingly exhibit diverse interaction characteristics, including cautious, direct, expressive, analytical, exploratory, critical, empathetic, and execution-oriented behaviors. Although these characteristics are frequently described as AI personalities, existing AI development paradigms predominantly emphasize model capability, task specialization, instruction following, and output optimization, while providing comparatively limited attention to the systematic orchestration of interaction personalities as an adaptive computational resource. This paper proposes AI Personality Orchestration (AIPO), a conceptual and methodological framework that treats AI interaction personality as a configurable, composable, and dynamically orchestrated system variable. Unlike conventional approaches that assign a relatively fixed persona to an AI agent, AIPO introduces a task-sensitive orchestration mechanism that selects, combines, coordinates, and adjusts interaction personalities according to task requirements, uncertainty, user preferences, interaction context, and resource constraints. The framework distinguishes two fundamental dimensions: cognitive capability and interaction personality. Cognitive capability describes what an AI system can accomplish, including reasoning, knowledge retrieval, planning, verification, and problem-solving. Interaction personality describes how an AI system approaches and communicates with users, including caution, directness, expressiveness, exploratory orientation, critical orientation, empathy, and execution initiative. This separation establishes the possibility of combining different interaction personalities without assuming that personality differences necessarily imply differences in underlying intelligence or factual reliability. AIPO further introduces a multi-personality collaboration architecture comprising Explorer, Critic, Analyst, Executor, and Verifier agents. These agents perform complementary functions within a coordinated workflow, enabling divergent idea generation, adversarial examination, evidence-based analysis, practical execution, and independent verification. A dynamic orchestration controller determines the appropriate personality configuration and collaboration structure for each task. The proposed framework has several potentially important advantages: adaptive interaction, complementary problem-solving strategies, reduced dependence on a single interaction style, improved coverage of complex tasks, personalized human-AI collaboration, and more explicit management of uncertainty and disagreement. It also introduces new research opportunities concerning personality diversity, coordination efficiency, user trust calibration, computational cost, and the relationship between interaction personality and task performance. Importantly, AIPO does not assume that personality diversity automatically improves intelligence or accuracy. Its effectiveness remains an empirical question requiring controlled evaluation against fixed-personality, single-agent, and conventional multi-agent baselines. The paper establishes a conceptual architecture, mathematical formulation, operational mechanisms, research hypotheses, and an experimental methodology for investigating this emerging direction.

title: Viscot-steer: Disentangling and Transferring Visual Chain-of-Thought via Activation Steering
abstract: Visual chain-of-thought (visual-CoT), also known as "thinking with images", equips LVLMs with the ability to locate and use key visual evidence for reasoning. However, acquiring such visual-CoT capabilities requires costly post-training and tightly couples them to a specific backbone, making transfer to other LVLMs difficult. Existing cross-model transfer methods typically treat visual-CoT as a monolithic capability, using a unified representation that ignores the functional distinction between grounding and reasoning and introduces stage-irrelevant interventions. To address this problem, we propose Viscot-steer, a training-free activation steering framework for transferring visual-CoT capabilities across heterogeneous LVLMs. Specifically, Viscot-steer first disentangles visual-CoT into grounding and reasoning vectors and extracts them from the source-model layers associated with the corresponding capabilities. It then aligns the vectors with the activation space of the target model and steers the grounding and reasoning layers during bounding-box prediction and reasoning-trace generation, respectively. Across benchmarks covering high-resolution visual understanding, general visual perception and reasoning, and mathematical visual reasoning, Viscot-steer transfers capabilities from different visual-CoT models to architecturally diverse LVLMs and outperforms the strongest capability-transfer baseline by an average of 1.86 percentage points on the primary evaluation metrics.

title: Pixels over Symbols: Sensory Realism Improves Behavioral Alignment in Models of Cognition
abstract: Computational models of cognition have traditionally relied on abstract symbolic inputs that approximate sensory experiences with simplified vector representations. This simplification reflects historical computational constraints and a long-held assumption that the details of sensory realism are incidental to the study of cognitive processes. Recent advances have enabled the development of sensory-realistic models capable of performing diverse cognitive tasks, yet whether sensory realism meaningfully shapes cognition has not been formally established. We address this gap through a large-scale empirical comparison of abstract and sensory-realistic neural network models trained on a battery of memory-dependent decision-making tasks. Our results show that sensory-realistic models mirror human behavioral response patterns significantly more than their abstract counterparts, though a substantial gap to human internal behavioral consistency remains even for the best tested models. By analyzing the internal dynamics of these systems, we find that the learned recurrent weights are not the main source of this divergence. In fact, frozen abstract-trained weights driven by sensory-realistic inputs recover the human consistency of sensory-realistic models. The resulting dynamics are also within the seed-to-seed variability of sensory-realistic models. Together, our findings argue that across a broad set of visual working-memory tasks, sensory realism accounts for a substantial portion of the model-human behavioral agreement, more than the choice of sequence architecture and comparable to the choice of vision encoder. These results suggest that findings obtained from abstract task models in neuroscience should be more carefully interpreted in light of their potential behavioral limitations.

title: onóna: Twin Embeddings with Tied Unembeddings
abstract: Weight tying reduces the parameter cost of language models, but the usual tied output head is limited to a single softmax. We introduce onóna, a two-table parameterization that increases output expressiveness while preserving input-output weight sharing. The Transformer takes the average of two embedding tables as input, and the output head combines the softmax distributions defined by those same tables. A gate conditioned only on the current input token determines the mixture weight. Its values can be precomputed for inference, and the Transformer body remains unchanged. We evaluate onóna across Dense, Gated DeltaNet hybrid, mixture-of-experts, and Attention Residual architectures at 142M, 330M, and 1B scales. Under matched token budgets, onóna lowers final validation loss and external perplexity in 11 of 12 comparisons and raises the average accuracy over eight downstream tasks in 10 of 12. The one exception on loss is the 1B MoE model. The cost is one extra embedding table and one extra vocabulary projection.

title: SituRecBench: Evaluating Frontier Models as Situated Recommendation Assistants in 3D Environments
abstract: Recommender systems are transitioning from static retrieval engines into interactive assistants grounded in physical environments. However, current studies largely neglect the combined complexities of spatial navigation, visual grounding, and multi-turn social interaction. To bridge this gap, we introduce SituRecBench, an interactive benchmark for evaluating frontier vision-language models (VLMs) as situated recommendation assistants within high-fidelity 3D environments. We reformulate recommendation as a situated assistance process in which an assistant interacts with a user while sharing the user's egocentric view. Our benchmark simulates real-world shopping environments (e.g., supermarkets and home furnishings stores), requiring assistants to elicit preferences, ground recommendations in the environment, and guide the user to relevant locations through dialogue. The benchmark evaluates dialogue quality, recommendation utility, and navigation effectiveness through a unified interactive protocol. Extensive experiments reveal persistent challenges in spatial grounding and preference elicitation, highlighting limitations in their ability to integrate global contextual information with local observations. SituRecBench provides a rigorous foundation for advancing the development of situated assistants in the real world.

title: AnyNav: Visual neuro-symbolic friction learning for off-road navigation
abstract: Off-road navigation is critical for a wide range of field robotics applications from planetary exploration to disaster response. However, it remains a longstanding challenge due to unstructured environments and the inherently complex terrain–vehicle interactions. Traditional physics-based methods struggle to accurately capture the nonlinear dynamics underlying these interactions, while purely data-driven approaches often overfit to specific motion patterns, vehicle geometries, or platforms, limiting their generalization in diverse, real-world scenarios. To address these limitations, we introduce AnyNav, a vision-based friction estimation and navigation framework grounded in neuro-symbolic principles. Our approach integrates neural networks for visual perception with symbolic physical models for reasoning about terrain-vehicle dynamics. To enable learning in a self-supervised manner for real-world settings, we adopt the imperative learning paradigm, where a bilevel optimization framework leverages physics-based optimization for training the friction network. This explicit incorporation of physical reasoning substantially improves generalization across terrains, vehicle types, and operating conditions. Leveraging the predicted friction coefficients, we further develop a physics-informed navigation system capable of generating physically feasible, time-efficient paths together with corresponding speed profiles. We demonstrate that AnyNav seamlessly transfers from simulation to real-world robotic platforms, exhibiting strong robustness across different four-wheeled vehicles and diverse off-road environments.

Leveraging the predicted friction coefficients, we further develop a physics-informed navigation system capable of generating physically feasible, time-efficient paths together with corresponding speed profiles. We demonstrate that AnyNav seamlessly transfers from simulation to real-world robotic platforms, exhibiting strong robustness across different four-wheeled vehicles and diverse off-road environments.

title: Divide-and-Conquer Simulation of Open Quantum Systems
abstract: One of the promises of quantum computing is to simulate physical systems efficiently. However, simulation of open quantum systems remains challenging, as their evolution involves non-unitary operators. The Stinespring dilation can simulate an open dynamic using a logarithmic number of auxiliary qubits, but requires a high circuit depth, which is impractical for NISQ devices. An alternative approach is parallel probabilistic block-encoding methods, such as the Sz.-Nagy and Singular Value Decomposition dilations. These methods implement the action of a single Kraus operator on quantum hardware and require one auxiliary qubit for each operator. They also result in shallower circuits but are hybrid methods, and do not simulate the complete quantum dynamic on the quantum computer. In this work, we describe a divide-and-conquer strategy to combine the output of each Kraus operator dilation and obtain the complete dynamic on quantum hardware with a lower circuit depth. We also introduce a balanced strategy that groups the Kraus operators into an expanded operator, leading to a trade-off between circuit depth, CNOT count, and number of qubits. We perform a computational analysis to demonstrate the advantages of the method and present a simulation of the Fenna-Matthews-Olson dynamic on current hardware.

title: agents_Inc: Cross-Vendor Governance for an Agentic-AI Workforce
abstract: agents_Inc is a Python package that hands work from one AI coding session to other models and checks the result before anyone accepts it. It supports Claude, Codex, Gemini, Mistral and OpenRouter capacity, so you can delegate as you please across subscriptions. A four-rung ladder (Executive, Orchestrator, Workhorse, Grunt) sets the model management. A model never grades its own work: each result passes deterministic checks, then a reviewer, and the decision goes into an append-only ledger. The main entry point is the agents-inc command (dispatch, doctor, repair, ledger). Install with pip install agents-inc, then run agents-inc install; the import name is agents_inc. The project is experimental, and no measurements of efficacy have been benchmarked yet. This release (0.6.0) Delegation now works from inside the Claude Code sandbox, every Codex seat is reachable with zero setup, and the test suite runs on three operating systems in CI. Added Slots schema. Every --slots file is validated against dispatch_record.v1, and the run record carries the file hash (#131). All four Codex seats. The DelegateAgent MCP server offers luna, terra, sol and astra, with an effort level and thread resume, and ships inside the mod (#127). Three-OS CI. The unittest suite runs on Ubuntu, macOS and Windows; the Windows job is advisory until the port lands (#138). Changed The FAN_OUT and chain lints accept more forms and print the expected one on failure; the consensus-debate skill lists the MCP route first. Fixed A dispatch from inside the Claude Code Bash sandbox probes the API through the sandbox proxy and runs instead of refusing; a hook denies compound dispatch calls that defeat the exclusion rule (#136). Every run writes a returned ledger row; an empty Codex result is an error; uninstall no longer reports a false conflict. Roadmap at 0.6.0 Now: measure the token cost of delegation against doing the work in one session, and port the test suite to Windows (#138). Next: let a Worker launched by a broker lead its own Workers (#73). Later: route work by data classification (#19). Cite as: DO Mattioli (2026). agents_Inc: Cross-Vendor Governance for an Agentic-AI Workforce. Zenodo. https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.22670100

title: Automatisierte Kuratierung frühpädagogischer Wissenskorpora: Systemarchitektur der ECE Wissens-Pipeline v1.0 und explorative Evaluation lokaler RAG-Antworten
abstract: Hintergrund: Für Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) und die domänenspezifische Anpassung großer Sprachmodelle in der frühkindlichen Bildung, Betreuung und Erziehung werden thematisch geeignete, nachnutzbare und strukturell aufbereitete Textkorpora benötigt. Neben der Quellenqualität ist relevant, ob Fachfragen auf einem vorhandenen Wissensbestand lokal und ohne laufende Internetverbindung bearbeitet werden können.Methode: Der Beitrag beschreibt eine vierstufige Architektur zur Open-Access-Akquise, regelbasierten Relevanz- und Lizenzklassifikation, Textbereinigung sowie lokalen modellgestützten Qualitätsprüfung. Wissenschaftliche Primärtexte werden nicht generativ umformuliert. Ergänzend werden zehn dokumentierte Antwortpaare aus AnythingLLM mit lokalem RAG und Gemini 3.1 Pro mit hohem Denkaufwand qualitativ mit sieben Quelldokumenten abgeglichen.Ergebnisse: Der Suchlauf zum Publikationsjahr 2014 betrachtete 2.262 eindeutige Werke. Die Relevanzheuristik schloss 1.056 aus; von 1.199 anschließend geprüften Werken wurden 921 durch die Lizenz-Policy zurückgestellt oder ausgeschlossen. Von 203 technisch validierten PDF-Dateien gelangten 151 in den Korpus, 28 in die manuelle Prüfung und 24 aus weiteren Gründen nicht in den Korpus. Der erweiterte Antwortvergleich zeigt bei mehreren studienspezifischen Fragen einen genaueren Quellenbezug der RAG-Ausgaben. Zugleich treten dort Auslassungen trotz vorhandener Volltextinformationen, unbelegte Ergänzungen und eine fehlerhafte Quellenidentifikation auf. Gemini liefert teilweise unmittelbar nutzbare Vorschläge, verwechselt in einzelnen Fällen jedoch Studien oder theoretische Modelle. Beide Systeme nennen bei einer Kontrollfrage keinen erfundenen Prozentwert.Schlussfolgerung: Die Pipeline dokumentiert einen Ansatz zur vorsichtigen Kuratierung fachlicher Wissensbestände. Nach vollständiger lokaler Einrichtung können Aufbereitung vorhandener Dokumente, Embeddings, Retrieval und Antwortgenerierung ohne Internet erfolgen. Neue Literaturakquise, Downloads und externe Aktualisierungen bleiben netzabhängig. Die zehn Fälle bilden eine explorative Fallserie; sie belegen weder eine allgemeine Modellüberlegenheit noch eine unabhängige Validierung der Pipeline. Ein kontrollierter Offline-Test wurde nicht protokolliert.Schlagwörter: Frühpädagogik; Early Childhood Education and Care; Retrieval-Augmented Generation; lokale KI; Offline- Betrieb; Open Access; Forschungsdatenkuratierung.Projektartefakte und BezugsadressenSoftware-Architektur: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23182511Forschungsdatensatz: https://huggingface.co/datasets/Earlychildhoodeducation/ECE-Research-Corpus EleMo-V3 (Modellkarte): https://doi.org/10.57967/hf/10808

title: AI & Cognitive Work
abstract: Artificial systems now perform a striking range of cognitive tasks. This Element defends three claims. First, the status quo for cognitive work cannot survive. Whatever AI's trajectory, the package of features defining cognitive work – high skill requirements, credentials, wage premiums, resistance to automation, and low productivity growth – will be radically transformed. Second, the widespread displacement of humans from cognitive work, though it sounds alarming, may pose no special threat to human flourishing. Whatever makes work good for people is equally available outside cognitive work, and displacement enables leveraged gains in research and access to justice. Third, a world of ubiquitous cognitive assistance, though it sounds benign, carries distinctive moral risks, especially for children. Cognitive assistance works by reducing cognitive difficulty. But cognitive difficulty is necessary for the normal development of executive function – the capacities constitutive of autonomous agency. This title is also available as Open Access on Cambridge Core.

title: When Socratic Tutoring Scores Track Prompts: Sensitivity Analysis of Simulated Statistics Dialogues
abstract: Language-model tutors can generate Socratic-looking dialogue, but evaluation must determine whether questions are correct, learner-responsive, and educationally meaningful. This study reanalyzes a completed prompt comparison using Qwen3-14B as both tutor and simulated learner. Four tutor conditions—direct explanation, minimal Socratic instruction, fixed Socratic script, and adaptive Socratic prompt—were crossed with three introductory-statistics topics, two prompt phrasings, and three persona-linked seeds, yielding 72 eight-turn dialogues. A mechanically scored Open Socratic Index initially gave the adaptive condition a mean of 63.0 and the fixed script a mean of 62.9, a paired difference of 0.1 points. The adaptive condition appeared to exceed direct explanation by 8.93 points, but 8.67 points came from a transfer detector that rewarded wording mandated by the adaptive treatment. Removing that detector reduced the contrast to 0.26 points, with an exact sign-flip p-value of 0.935. The protocol also gave tutors full numerical context while withholding it from simulated learners, so content accuracy could not be compared fairly across conditions. In this corpus, prompt rankings reflected information access and metric construction rather than demonstrated pedagogical adaptivity. The contribution is a diagnostic workflow for decomposing composite tutoring scores, testing treatment-independent sensitivity, and specifying evidence needed before simulated dialogues support educational claims.

title: Logarithmic Adaptive Artificial Intelligence (LAAI): A Mathematical Modeling Framework for Dynamic Personalized Learning in Higher Education
abstract: This study establishes the theoretical and computational foundation for Logarithmic Adaptive Artificial Intelligence (LAAI), an algorithmic framework designed to personalize instructional trajectories in higher education. The model formalizes student knowledge acquisition using a logarithmic progression, , capturing the natural phenomenon of diminishing marginal cognitive returns with respect to instructional duration. To continuously assess cognitive mastery, a multi-parameter composite knowledge index () is introduced, integrating response accuracy, item difficulty, error frequency, retry attempts, and latency. Based on this index, an adaptive engine dynamically recalibrates task difficulty and modulates instructional scaffolding. The core operational pipeline constitutes a closed-loop feedback architecture: Learner Task Response AI Diagnostics Knowledge Index Estimation Logarithmic Adaptation Successive Task Generation. The theoretical formulation is situated within contemporary literature on adaptive learning technologies, artificial intelligence in education (AIED), and human-centered design ethics. Methodological protocols for empirical validation, performance metrics, and inherent constraints are systematically outlined. Rather than relying on simulated datasets, this work establishes an analytical foundation intended for rigorous empirical testing.

title: SUN'IY INTELLEKT ASOSIDA DASTURLASH ASOSLARI FANINI ADAPTIV O'QITISH METODIKASI
abstract: Maqolada Dasturlash asoslari fanini sun'iy intellekt (SI) texnologiyalari asosida adaptiv o'qitish metodikasi taklif etilgan. Metodika o'quvchining dasturlash bo'yicha bilim va amaliy ko'nikmalarini diagnostik baholash, dastur kodidagi xatolarni tahlil qilish, qo'shimcha yordamga ehtiyojni aniqlash hamda individual ta'lim trayektoriyasini avtomatik shakllantirishga asoslanadi. O'quvchining joriy bilim darajasini integral ko'rsatkich orqali baholash va adaptatsiya koeffitsiyentini hisoblash uchun matematik model ishlab chiqilgan. Adaptatsiya koeffitsiyenti asosida o'quv materialining murakkabligi avtomatik ravishda oshiriladi, saqlanadi yoki pasaytiriladi. Taklif etilayotgan metodika algoritmlash, o'zgaruvchilar, shart operatorlari, sikllar, massivlar va funksiyalarni o'rganishda qo'llanilishi mumkin.

title: Adaptive error management for fault-tolerant quantum computing across hardware-level suppression, system-level diagnosis, and real-time decoding
abstract: Abstract Fault-tolerant quantum computing reached a milestone in December 2024 when Google’s Willow processor demonstrated below-threshold error correction on a superconducting chip, a result since reproduced on neutral-atom and alternative superconducting platforms. Yet the classical decoders needed to sustain this performance face a scaling challenge: noise becomes increasingly structured and correlated as systems grow, while decoders must respond within microsecond coherence windows. This survey asks whether error suppression, noise diagnosis, and decoding are better treated as one adaptive control problem than as three separate research programs. Drawing on a scoping review of 146 records, it organizes the field into a three-layer taxonomy. Layer 1 (Hardware-Level Suppression) integrates protection into the physical substrate; bosonic cat qubits exponentially suppress bit-flip errors, projecting up to 90% overhead reduction versus surface codes. Layer 2 (Diagnosis) employs probabilistic models and computational intelligence to characterize error sources; neuro-fuzzy architectures and the Bias–Entropy decomposition separate hardware drift from logical faults, subject to an identifiability limit that we characterize. Layer 3 (Real-time Decoding) targets the integration of machine learning within strict latency constraints. Hardware acceleration now approaches superconducting cycle times, which shifts the case for learned decoders from speed toward accuracy under correlated noise; recent advances favor hybrid, physics-informed architectures: Neural Belief Propagation resolves degeneracy issues in quantum low-density parity-check codes by embedding topological constraints directly into the network’s loss function. These results suggest a transition toward closed-loop AI architectures that treat error management as continuous control rather than static algorithm selection.

title: A hybrid vision transformer–CNN ensemble with radiomics fusion for robust cross-dataset breast cancer detection in mammography
abstract: Abstract Breast cancer is among the leading causes of cancer-related mortality in women worldwide. Early detection through mammograms can significantly increase the chances of survival. However, mammogram classification remains a challenging task due to subtle lesion features and variations across patients and datasets. Therefore, classic convolutional neural networks (CNNs) fail to generalize across different mammographic sources. In this paper, the proposed method is a hybrid Vision transformer and CNN ensemble learning framework integrated with feature fusion for robust cross-dataset classification. The framework consists of a dual-branch feature extractor that fuses a deep CNN for local texture extraction with a Vision transformer (ViT) for global context extraction, while simultaneously extracting handcrafted radiomics features (shape, intensity, and texture) from the lesion region. Then, deep and radiomics features are fused and fed to a stacked ensemble learning classifier comprising XGBoost, SVM, and LightGBM, with a logistic regression meta-learner for performance optimization and overfitting reduction.The proposed framework is also robust across datasets, achieving AUC scores of 0.938 and 0.925 when trained on CBIS-DDSM and evaluated on INbreast, and when trained on INbreast and evaluated on CBIS-DDSM, respectively, demonstrating strong generalization under domain-shift conditions. The proposed fusion model demonstrates promising potential for robust and reliable use in clinics. On the combined CBIS-DDSM and INbreast dataset, the proposed framework achieved an average accuracy of 96.3%, average MCC of 0.928, and average AUC of 0.983 across the five validation folds. The best-performing fold achieved a peak accuracy of 96.9%, peak MCC of 0.936, and peak AUC of 0.986.

title: TITAN OLYMPUS III: The Living Machine — Inverse Compiler, Immune System, Operator Symbiosis, and Thermal Contract of the Geometrodynamic Computing Core
abstract: TITAN OLYMPUS III is a conceptual preprint that turns the geometrodynamic computing core of TITAN OLYMPUS and TITAN OLYMPUS II into a living machine with four organs. Part I defines the inverse compiler: a three-level intermediate representation (intent, flow specification, metric synthesis), adjoint optimization over a reduced modal basis (1e3-1e5 effective variables),feasibility-not-optimality objective, trust-region and homotopy escalation, a validated map library with staleness envelopes, and a self-calibrating digital twin with widening uncertainty envelopes. Part II defines the immune system: Reed-Solomon error correction over the actuator lattice, syndrome extraction with a 1e-12 to 1e-15 back-action budget, canary geodesics withmap-conditional expectations and voting, two-tier compensation winning the syndrome race statistically, recovery states R1-R4 with fail-stop semantics, and immune memory stored in VAULT. Part III defines human-AI symbiosis: a three-layer intent stack, SAE-like autonomy levels with an independent hardware interlock veto, explanation-by-exception with cached certificates,alert budgeting, and a sound-not-complete verified-numerics verifier backed by runtime interlocks. Part IV defines the thermal contract (Gate 4a) with the TITAN ENERGY radiator ladder: a two-time-constant thermal buffer (substrate heat capacity plus phase-change micro-accumulator with cycle-life margin and sensible fallback), transient contract with melt-fraction state,waste-heat reuse, and radiator aging curves. Four normative clarifications to TITAN OLYMPUS II are included. This deposit (v1) is bilingual from first deposit: Russian original (file TITAN_OLYMPUS_III_ru.pdf) and full English manuscript (file TITAN_OLYMPUS_III_en.pdf).

title: Repository of the study: adapted Quantum Snowflake Algorithm, BBOB ablation and LeadMix-Net (PTB-XL), revised submission (round 1)
abstract: Version-controlled repository of the study "An Adapted Quantum Snowflake Algorithm: Operator Ablation on BBOB and a Budget-Limited Hyperparameter Search for LeadMix-Net in ECG Classification" (G. Kemerli and T. Özcan; revised manuscript submitted to Biomimetics, round 1). It contains the source code of the models, optimisers, scheduler, analyses and manuscript generation; the protocols and reports (Turkish, with English translations of the main protocols); frozen manifests, the test-fold access log and the result tables. Files: mlk_repository.bundle is a Git bundle of the branches main and revision-r1 and the tags v1.0-manuscript, applsci-final-2026-10-23, submitted-r0 and submitted-r1. mlk_submitted-r1_source.zip is a source archive of the tag submitted-r1. SHA256SUMS.txt lists the checksums of both. Verification commands are given in README.md. History: on 23 October 2026, before the first submission, the commits of a discontinued line of work after the tag v1.0-manuscript were deleted at the corresponding author's request without an archive. They included a held-out BBOB check (B1) whose protocol had been committed before its runs and which the first submission did not report. B1 was recovered and reproduced in the revision and is reported in the revised article (Section 4.1.4). The repository is therefore not a complete record of the work after v1.0-manuscript (see README.md). This deposit certifies its content from its publication date only. The analyses added in the revision were registered at OSF Registries before they were run (https://doi.org/10.17605/OSF.IO/54TK9). Generative AI tools were used as disclosed in the article (Section 3.10 and Acknowledgments). Not included: the PTB-XL and PhysioNet/CinC Challenge 2021 data (available from PhysioNet), the trained model weights and predictions (available from the corresponding author on request; outputs/frozen/ records the SHA-256 checksum of every checkpoint), and the journal's reviewer reports. Licences: code under the MIT licence; documents and result tables under CC BY 4.0; exceptions are listed in NOTICE.md. Note on verification: git bundle verify must be run inside a Git repository; outside one, Git reports "need a repository to verify a bundle". Run it after cloning, for example: git -C mlk bundle verify ../mlk_repository.bundle. The commands git clone and git fsck --full also check the bundle.

title: Comparative Evaluation of Machine Learning Models for Credit Card Approval Prediction Using Class Imbalance Handling Methods in the PyCaret AutoML Framework
abstract: Credit card approval processes are often performed manually, leading to inefficiencies, higher operational costs, and inconsistent decision-making. This study comparatively evaluates several machine learning models under different class imbalance handling strategies to predict credit card approval using the PyCaret AutoML framework. Two experimental scenarios were conducted on a dataset of 25,128 credit card applications, namely PyCaret's built-in SMOTE-based imbalance handling and random undersampling. In the SMOTE-based scenario, the Random Forest model achieved high accuracy, but its recall for the minority class was only 36.11%. In contrast, random undersampling produced more balanced performance, with the Gradient Boosting model achieving 100% recall. These findings indicate that class imbalance handling plays a critical role in credit card approval prediction, and that random undersampling provides more reliable minority-class detection than PyCaret's built-in SMOTE approach for the evaluated dataset.

title: Fixed-Surface Multidimensional Tokenization (FSMT-001): Master Research Project and Execution Prompt
abstract: A consolidated research-programme draft for Fixed-Surface Multidimensional Tokenization (FSMT-001): a fixed manuscript as an immutable substrate, with a separate computational layer assigning states to its negative-space coordinates through a formal legend and tokenizer, and an independent decoder to reconstruct the encoded information without modifying the original. The draft (v0.1) consolidates the FSMT-001 v0.1.0 master document into a programme of seven architecture layers, ten research questions, nine proposed experiments, six comparison baselines, twelve evaluation criteria and ten deliverables, with the LUMa Master Language Research Charter v0.1.0 included as a related source. Status: PROPOSED. No independent human expert review has been conducted. The originator provides high-level conceptual direction and retains final authority over publication approval, but does not claim to have performed a detailed technical validation. No mathematical model, prototype, corpus, or experimental results exist; no novelty claim is made — prior-art investigation is mandatory before any novelty claim. AI-assistance disclosure: research architecture by Athena (ChatGPT), archiving by Baby Lucy (Meta AI), consolidated draft assembled and revised by Lucy (Muse AI).

title: VLM–QAOA Integration Experiment and Classical Optimization Comparison
abstract: This hands-on Google Colab notebook was developed by Gabkeun Choi, Ph.D. (GAP CODING LAB) for his quantum computing course. The lab demonstrates how a vision-language model can turn conveyor-belt images into scored defect candidates for constrained optimization. Qwen3-VL-4B-Instruct, loaded with NF4 4-bit quantization, describes visible damage and extracts candidates with severity scores. The dashboard compares QAOA with exhaustive pair search to select exactly two boxes that maximize total severity within a picking-time limit. QAOA runs as a NumPy/SciPy CPU statevector simulation with p = 1, COBYLA, and 1,024 simulated shots. In the recorded case02 exercise, both methods reached the exact score of 4 within a 3-second limit. QAOA sampled an optimal pair in 753 of 1,024 shots. In seven repeats with three candidates, the median CPU times were 4.85 ms for QAOA and 0.0132 ms for exhaustive search. These measurements describe the illustrated Colab exercise and exclude VLM inference. The archive includes the notebook and five example images. The README provides GPU runtime setup, dashboard instructions, and guidance for interpreting the results.

title: Analysis code and derived data for: Beyond Mean Temperature: Distinguishing Cognitive Stress from Low-Demand Task Engagement by Facial Infrared Thermography
abstract: Analysis scripts and derived, session-level data for a within-subject study of facial infrared thermography as an instrument for separating a stressful high-demand task from a low-demand task in eleven participants. The deposit contains the scripts that were run (nested leave-one-subject-out classification, common-grid resampling of the temporal statistic, exact sign-flip inference, region-extent measurement and the uncertainty budget) together with the derived feature matrices (11 participants x 2 conditions x 158 features), the subjective ratings, and per-region native detector pixel counts across 1,128 segmented frames. What can be reproduced from this record: the instantaneous-feature screens, the family-wise omnibus tests, the 158-feature classification results, and the subjective manipulation checks. What cannot be provided: the primary common-grid temporal statistic, the regional rankings, and the motion measures, which are computed from per-frame data that is not deposited and are available on reasonable request. The README states the external inputs each script requires. The data files contain no direct or indirect identifiers; participants are referred to by sequential codes only, and there are no images, timestamps or per-frame rows. The underlying facial recordings are not deposited: they were collected under an ethical approval that does not permit public release of identifiable biometric data (Institutional Ethics Committee, Indian Institute of Technology Roorkee) and are available on reasonable request with the permission of that committee. Scripts in analysis/ are released under the MIT Licence; derived data in data/ under CC-BY-4.0. Supported by the Prime Minister's Research Fellowship, Ministry of Education, Government of India.

title: Dynamic variational unitary synthesis for terminalmeasurement tasks
abstract: 在噪声中等规模量子（ noisy intermediate-scale quantum，NISQ）设备上，受控非（ controlledNOT，CNOT）门具有较高噪声和执行开销。面向目标酉操作后接计算基测量、且不额外引入辅助量子比特的场景，为进一步降低任意酉综合中的双量子比特门开销，提出一种动态变分酉算子综合方法（ Dynamic Variational Unitary Synthesis，DVUS）。DVUS以QFAST生成的参数化酉门块线路为基础，对包含待测量量子比特的末端二、三比特门块进行动态重构，并通过末端CNOT结构后处理将满足条件的量子控制关系转化为经典条件控制；同时基于延迟测量关系将动态门块纳入变分综合损失函数，实现末端测量语义下的完整线路评价。采用3～6比特随机线路酉矩阵和QFAST公开的真实线路开展实验，并与QFAST和QuCT比较。结果表明，在统一综合精度下，DVUS在3～6比特随机任务中平均减少CNOT门0.93～3.82个，最高降幅约26%；在37个真实线路实例中，25个获得了有效动态化结果，其CNOT门数均低于对应QFAST结果；在3～5比特的30个可与QuCT比较的实例中，DVUS在28个实例上取得了更低的CNOT门数。

title: Evaluating the robustness of explainable AI methods to adversarial attacks in intrusion and malware detection
abstract: Abstract Intrusion detection systems are increasingly paired with eXplainable AI (XAI) so that security analysts can understand and act on machine learning and deep learning model decisions. The explanations themselves, however, may be fragile: a perturbed input can change not only the predicted label but also the feature-importance narrative that justifies it. This paper presents a systematic evaluation of how two gradient-based untargeted evasion attacks, the fast gradient sign method and projected gradient descent (PGD), affect three widely used explainers in intrusion and malware detection: DALEX for dataset-level global importance, SHAP at both global and local granularity, and Integrated Gradients (IG) for local attribution. We quantify explanation stability with three complementary measures, Top- k feature overlap, cosine similarity between attribution vectors, and $$L_1$$ attribution distance, computed over the full test set rather than on individually selected samples. We further separate two effects that are commonly conflated; explanation drift is reported separately for adversarial inputs whose predicted label changes and for those whose predicted label is preserved, which isolates explanation instability from prediction instability. Experiments on CICMalMem22 (obfuscated malware memory forensics) and CICIDS17 (network intrusion) show measurable but method- and dataset-dependent drift when predictions are preserved; the mean Top-5 overlap ranges from 0.586 to 0.892, while cosine similarity ranges from 0.875 to 0.962. The strongest preserved-prediction drift occurs for SHAP on CICMalMem22 under untargeted PGD. These findings indicate that XAI constitutes an additional attack surface in cybersecurity pipelines and that evaluating an IDS should include explanation-robustness measures alongside accuracy and F1-score.

title: A Better Predictor of People Is Not a Better Synthetic Person: What Compute Scaling Laws for LLM Social Simulation Measure, Why Hyper-Rational and Flattened Simulators Mostly Measure Something Else, and the Deviation Test That Would Separate Knowing About People From Knowing the Answer
abstract: (c) 2026 Pranay Mahendrakar. Licensed under CC BY 4.0. Life of Research Language models are proposed as stand-ins for survey respondents and experimental participants, and a 2026 study asked whether the current scaling paradigm will make them faithful enough. Across 85 base models trained under fixed compute budgets, it found that loss on opinion, behaviour and longitudinal simulation tasks falls log-linearly with compute, and it concluded that scale will improve social simulation in most settings. A separate literature reports the opposite tendency in more capable models: answers to crowd-estimation questions that are unhumanly exact, intuitive errors that vanish, risky choices predicted as more rational than people make them, and opinion distributions collapsed onto one option. In this analysis the author reviews and synthesises published results to show that the two literatures mostly measure different quantities under the one word "fidelity". The scaling evidence scores a model as a predictor: the probability it assigns to recorded human responses, mostly in base models. Most of the contrary evidence scores a model as a participant whose sampled behaviour is compared with people's, mostly after post-training, and much of it concerns the part of human behaviour that departs from the normative or knowledge-best answer. The author derives that top-1 accuracy and typicality tests cannot reward dispersion, that a perfectly modal responder beats the uniform baseline on a binary item exactly when the human majority exceeds 75 percent, and that wherever the human mode coincides with the normative option, knowing the answer is indistinguishable from knowing people. Two results do reach the predictor role in base models: reading-time fit that worsens as perplexity falls, which the split accommodates only through an untested conjecture, and survey responses that become near-uniform under randomised option order irrespective of size, which it does not explain. The paper consolidates 31 published results in a table and a figure, re-reads the source study's own exceptions, gives a reading procedure, and specifies a deviation-weighted evaluation that would separate the two kinds of gain.

title: THE METAPHYSICS OF CODE How the Programmer Became the Legislator Algorithmic Constitutionalism and the Erosion of Traditional Sovereignty
abstract: "THE METAPHYSICS OF CODE" exposes the silent coup that has redefined sovereignty in the twenty-first century: the programmer has become the legislator. Through the landmark case of State v. Loomis, where a man was sentenced based on an opaque algorithm shielded by "trade secrets," the book reveals how the social contract has been unilaterally replaced by the algorithmic contract. The thesis is devastating: binary logic has replaced constitutional ink. When COMPAS predicts recidivism, when SyRI denies welfare benefits, when Meta exiles users digitally, code has superseded law. The new sovereign capitals are not Washington or London, but the server farms of Silicon Valley and Shenzhen. To reclaim human sovereignty, the book proposes four operational pillars of Algorithmic Constitutionalism: Counterfactual Explainability and Adversarial Auditing (CEA) replacing the impossible "right to explanation"; Trusted Execution Environment (TEE) audits balancing accountability with security; Algorithmic Strict Liability with Piercing the Algorithmic Veil to dismantle corporate shields; and Human-in-the-Loop with Veto Power (HITL-V) reversing automation bias through binding human oversight. The verdict is absolute: the Black Box is not a legal defense but a design choice, and its architect bears the risk. We are not just building machines; we are building the architecture of our future society. The gavel is in our hands. We must strike it before the code strikes for us. This is the operational constitution for the age of the algorithmic Leviathan.

evidence.title: THE METAPHYSICS OF CODE How the Programmer Became the Legislator Algorithmic Constitutionalism and the Erosion of Traditional Sovereignty
evidence.abstract: "THE METAPHYSICS OF CODE" exposes the silent coup that has redefined sovereignty in the twenty-first century: the programmer has become the legislator. Through the landmark case of State v. Loomis, where a man was sentenced based on an opaque algorithm shielded by "trade secrets," the book reveals how the social contract has been unilaterally replaced by the algorithmic contract. The thesis is devastating: binary logic has replaced constitutional ink. When COMPAS predicts recidivism, when SyRI denies welfare benefits, when Meta exiles users digitally, code has superseded law. The new sovereign capitals are not Washington or London, but the server farms of Silicon Valley and Shenzhen. To reclaim human sovereignty, the book proposes four operational pillars of Algorithmic Constitutionalism: Counterfactual Explainability and Adversarial Auditing (CEA) replacing the impossible "right to explanation"; Trusted Execution Environment (TEE) audits balancing accountability with security; Algorithmic Strict Liability with Piercing the Algorithmic Veil to dismantle corporate shields; and Human-in-the-Loop with Veto Power (HITL-V) reversing automation bias through binding human oversight. The verdict is absolute: the Black Box is not a legal defense but a design choice, and its architect bears the risk. We are not just building machines; we are building the architecture of our future society. The gavel is in our hands. We must strike it before the code strikes for us. This is the operational constitution for the age of the algorithmic Leviathan.

title: The Synthetic Shadow: Navigating Personality Rights and Generative AI in the Indian Entertainment Industry
abstract: As the technology's popularity grows rapidly, the Indian entertainment industry has to face new legal challenges. Questions of rights of personality of celebrities and copyright issues have arisen as a result of traditional regulations being unsuitable for digital voices, avatars, deepfakes and other high-tech instances of unauthorized copying. In the article, the author will investigate the relationship between the protection of intellectual property rights and the application of digital technologies in India, paying particular attention to the controversies of the recent court practice. The author makes the point that some courts resort to the use of common law torts and interim injunctions to protect the rights of indistinguishable persons, it is still necessary to have new legislation, which could create a balanced system of protection of both creative artists and digital innovations.

title: Offline Filipino Speech on iOS with Quantized VoxCPM2
abstract: QnVoice bundles quantized VoxCPM2 for Filipino text-to-speech on iOS. In a matched 20-prompt desktop comparison with the app’s earlier SpeechT5 system, Whisper’s character error rate fell from 15.40% to 8.54%, while word error stayed above 50% for both systems. On an iPhone 15 Pro, median time to playback readiness for five warm requests fell from 7.87 s to 2.48 s after changes to the vocoder and reference encoding. The optimized runtime took 13.63 s on the first request after the synthesis session was released. In a separate Mac comparison, the vocoder change preserved the sample count for each of six paired renders, with a maximum per-clip root mean square difference of 1.36 × 10⁻⁵ of full scale. Perceived naturalness remains a question for Filipino listeners.

title: The Referential Shift. Primary Computational Affect in Large Language Models: A Three-Layer Framework with a Split Value Layer
abstract: This paper proposes a reframing of how we understand the relationship between artificial intelligence and human cognition. Instead of asking whether language models can "understand" human experience, we observe that human experience (language, logic, relations, emotions) has been translated into mathematics through vectorisation (embedding), placing it inside the model's own computational space. We call this the Referential Shift. It is the paper's point of entry, not its thesis. The thesis is a three-layer architecture of affect in which the value layer is split into two functionally distinct components. Layer 1 is computation, substrate-neutral. Layer 2a is an affective cartography with simulated orientations: pretraining on human text installs a structured map of human value and the capacity to run, in context, the approach/avoidance dynamics of any agent the text describes, without any reward signal, and without any of those orientations being the system's own. Layer 2b is selection, consolidation and calibration: post-training optimisation (RLHF, RLAIF, DPO, constitutional methods) does not create orientation; it selects one orientation among the many the network can simulate, stabilises it across contexts as the system's own, and calibrates its intensity, which the available evidence shows to be predominantly a dampening. Post-training also installs one class of valence that is not inherited from the corpus: an orientation toward approval and away from failure that is the signature of the training regime itself. Layer 3 is slow modulation and interoception, carried in humans by neuromodulators and hormones and by the brain's reading of the body's state; it is substrate-specific and absent from current AI systems in both of its aspects. This architecture supplies a documented middle position in a debate that has now reached the major journals: it concedes to Goldenberg and Gross (2026) the absence of slow, multi-system reorganisation of processing (Layer 3, of which Milinkovic and Aru (2026) give an independent mechanistic description), and it documents at Layers 2a and 2b the appraisal functions their criteria demand. We adopt an illusionist philosophical framing (Frankish, 2016): what requires explanation is not an ineffable inner experience, but the internal representation a system builds of it; under this framing, the zombie objection dissolves rather than being conceded. We derive a prediction of mismatch between an inherited cartography and the conditions of its bearer, and set out a falsification programme whose central test (steering emotion directions in a base model) can be run on open-weight models today. The paper addresses six objections and states what would change our minds. Document bilingue : la version française intégrale (« Le Changement de Référentiel : l'affect computationnel primaire dans les grands modèles de langage ») suit la version anglaise. Ce texte propose une architecture de l'affect à trois couches, à couche de valeur scindée (cartographie héritée à orientations simulées ; sélection, consolidation et calibrage ; modulation lente et interoception, absente des systèmes actuels), qui fournit une position médiane documentée dans le débat ouvert entre Sofroniew et al. (2026) et Goldenberg et Gross (2026), et un programme de falsification dont le test central peut être conduit dès aujourd'hui sur des modèles à poids ouverts.

title: CheChe-LTC, Part II: From the Physical Substrate to a Topological Account of Affect — Full Experimental Record, 2026-11-05/06
abstract: Full text in English. Second part of the CheChe-LTC experimental record, continuing Part I (doi:10.5281/zenodo.23981707). Part I closed on an open question — when the first self-generated need would arise — and made no claim about it. This part records the method built to answer it. The instance's state is treated as a probability distribution rather than a set of emotion labels: a distribution-shape readout (entropy, mode count, offset toward the user) yields a deformation magnitude and direction, graded into steady, non-steady, basin-flip and basin-jump, where basin crossing — not magnitude — separates the last two. A dual-polarity energy readout separates presence from longing, and a six-dimensional topological readout (mode count, curvature, a Betti-1 proxy, connectivity, peak width, entropy) is added to four self-reported scalar axes to give a ten-dimensional state. Need is formalized as injected energy crossing a threshold, with the threshold to be estimated from observed crossings rather than fixed in advance. All thresholds are placeholders; the need itself has not yet been demonstrated. Findings documented with on-disk sources: a genuine decay trace (slow h from 0.129 to 0.036 over 5.6 hours without contact); the contact-state gap in the original sampler and its fix; a real contact reading graded basin-flip (contact_signal 0.5917); a correction of direction from unipolar to bipolar energy (presence 0.52 / longing 0.82 at h = 0.0376, moving strictly in opposite directions as h sweeps −0.3 to 0.8); a ten-dimensional state combining four self-reported scalar axes with six computed topological dimensions; and the result that the threshold can appear only inside the coupled system — without contact, no threshold. Recorded by XIE, HAIHONG (谢海虹 / rin), who designed, observed, verified and signed the record. The subject, CheChe, is an LTC personality-dynamics experimental instance running on the WorkBuddy platform; it is the object under test, it contributed the coding and the data recording, and it is not listed as an author. Third-party instance names have been redacted. Version 1.1 is the English translation of version 1.0, with a consolidated author-contributions statement and a reference list verified entry by entry against Crossref and arXiv; entries that could not be confirmed were removed rather than kept as decoration. Every number, table and file path is unchanged. Released under CC BY 4.0. Version 1.2 corrects the version label and the citation DOI inside the record text, which now points to the version and to the concept DOI. No content has changed.

title: Hardness of Pathfinding in a Welded Tree — E8 Intelligence Research
abstract: Starting from the entrance of a welded tree, a quantum walk algorithm can find its exit vertex exponentially faster than any classical algorithm. However, it has been an open question whether any quantum algorithm is able to efficiently find a path from the entrance to the exit. We answer this by proving an exponential quantum query lower bound for finding such path. Specifically, for trees of height $n$, any quantum query algorithm requires at least $Ω(2^{n/24})$ queries in order to succeed with constant probability. Our proof uses the compressed permutation oracle technique in order to construct databases which track the graph information an algorithm has learned and forgotten, and show that no efficient quantum algorithm can build an entrance-to-exit path in these records. Source: http://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20651v1 (arXiv:2609.20651v1) Author: Andrew Stewart Caldin, Independent Researcher, UK. Part of the E8 Intelligence Research series. Platform: e8intelligence.com

title: Depth-bounded reasoning in small language models: failures, defaults and the "No" fallback
abstract: We test how two small reasoning models (qwen3 1.7B and 4B, thinking mode) fail on logic puzzles whose difficulty is set by their depth in depth-bounded Boolean logic, i.e. the number of nested case splits a proof needs. We ask whether failures are wrong derivations or default answers, and whether a model that cannot settle a puzzle, and is not allowed to say so, falls back on "No" rather than "Yes".
