title: AR-Edit: Training-Free Autoregressive Video Editing without Inversion
abstract: Editing a video stream in real time, without access to future frames, is essential for interactive applications. Existing training-free video editing methods, however, assume full offline access to the entire sequence, while streaming approaches either rely on additional training or are limited to specific editing techniques. We show that this limitation can be removed by analyzing the self-attention dynamics of DMD-distilled autoregressive (AR) video diffusion models. We uncover a key asymmetry: queries and keys remain stable and aligned with their source counterparts across denoising timesteps, while values diverge and encode the evolving content. Inherited from the non-distilled bidirectional teacher, this asymmetry is strongest at high noise, where few-step streaming models operate. The resulting mechanism is simple: a single forward pass suffices to capture source identity in the value features, which can be reused throughout generation. Starting from pure Gaussian noise and injecting only these source values reconstructs the input with fidelity matching or surpassing inversion-based methods, effectively eliminating inversion. Based on this insight, we introduce AR-Edit, a training-free, inversion-free method that caches source values once and selectively injects them during denoising. Across multiple AR backbones, AR-Edit enables real-time streaming editing with superior source preservation and tonal fidelity at minimal overhead.

title: e-means: outperforming k-means (in one-tenth the epochs)
abstract: Lloyd's k-means algorithm is a long-running standard for clustering, with applications in data analysis, retrieval, quantization and data curation. In this paper, we introduce an exponential moving average optimization procedure for k-means with mini-batch updates, powered by modern deep learning machinery and new insights. We also establish scaling laws on how decay rate and batch size impact final performance. This gives us a formulaic rule to fix them for multiple problem sizes and embedding datasets, without the need for any hyperparameter sweep. The resulting clustering algorithm, coined e-means, is much faster than Lloyd k-means and converges to lower losses, frequently even beating k-means++. On a wide array of embeddings datasets, it beats the loss of Lloyd k-means at 25 epochs in 1.4 to 2.6 epochs, which translates to 10-45x GPU wall-clock speedups compared to state-of-the-art k-means implementations. As an example, e-means partitions DINO10B, a dataset of 10 billion DINO embeddings, into 16 million clusters in only 2.5 epochs, reaching a loss below Lloyd's at 25 epochs.

title: Richness Is Not Evenness: Ordered Renyi Crossings under Self-Training
abstract: Recursive self-training of language models, a setting studied in model collapse, can reduce vocabulary while making frequent words, mostly function words, less dominant. We fine-tune English GPT-2 on its own output for nine generations, vary the training-data sampling temperature, and measure every model with one fixed sampler. As training temperature rises, Renyi entropy changes turn from loss to gain at distinct temperatures: min-entropy first, then collision entropy, Shannon entropy and observed richness. Between the outer crossings, word types fall while the most-common word becomes less dominant. Untruncated training at T = 1 lies in this interval: at 13,000 words, generation 9 has 24% fewer types than generation 0 yet collision entropy is 0.91 bits higher. The ordering persists with a finer grid, different measurement samplers, a fixed word budget and five fresh training seeds. Min-entropy again crosses before richness in four further settings (in Hindi only at interpolated roots) and in 12 of 13 distinct measurements under eight text representations. Next-token identities and a categorical simulation isolate decoding and sampling effects; the crossing order remains empirical. Fine-tuning on human text can produce the same split while likelihood improves, and no single order's sign reliably identifies worse likelihood across the tested settings. We recommend reporting entropy profiles at stated budgets with an independent quality measure.

title: A novel cost-effective layout-aware quantum circuit synthesis of symmetric functions on triangular, square, and heavy-hex layouts
abstract: Abstract The quantum layout and the mapping of logical to physical qubits are crucial in quantum circuit synthesis for a real quantum computer. In particular, circuits containing large n -bit Toffoli gates ( $$n>3$$ ), such as those derived from cost-expensive gate constructions and hard-to-decompose Exclusive-or Sum of Products (ESOP) expressions, have complications with effective mappings into contemporary quantum layouts, including square grid and heavy-hex layouts. These complications are primarily caused by the limited connectivity among the physical qubits in such layouts, leading to the addition of many SWAP gates. This paper presents several contributions to address these challenges for cost-effectively constructing circuits for totally, generalized, and conditionally symmetric functions. Firstly, we introduce a novel quantum circuit synthesis methodology for such functions based on Reed–Muller Lattices, leveraging Positive and Negative Davio expansions as intermediate representations. Secondly, we present the SWAT gate, a composite operation consisting of a 2-qubit SWAP gate followed by a 3-qubit Toffoli gate, designed to reduce mapping overhead. Thirdly, we demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach on existing industrial quantum architectures by achieving cost-efficient mappings onto square grid and heavy-hex quantum layouts without introducing additional SWAP gates when using the SWAT gate. Finally, we introduce a speculative triangular layout and corresponding layout-aware circuit constructions, serving as a theoretical framework for evaluating synthesis efficiency under enhanced connectivity assumptions. Overall, our research, benchmarked against ESOP-based and BDD-based synthesis methods, demonstrates that Reed–Muller Lattices provide a powerful approach for the layout-aware quantum circuit synthesis of symmetric and related functions, with significant potential to reduce mapping overhead in near-term quantum architectures.

title: Seeing What Matters: Benchmarking Task-Conditioned Actionable Spatial Belief for Manipulation
abstract: When should a robot look at the cup, and when at the portafilter? Spatial-reasoning benchmarks evaluate whether a model can describe a scene, but manipulation needs something more specific: the ability to acquire the particular evidence that makes the current command executable. A view that is informative for one task can be useless for another, even at the same workstation. We introduce Seeing What Matters, a benchmark for task-conditioned actionable spatial belief in simulated tabletop manipulation. Across three domains--coffee workstation, drawer/cabinet, and microwave/appliance--the benchmark provides 860 frozen evaluation cases; expanding across methods, budgets, and inference repeats yields more than 115,000 evaluator episodes under two protocols: closed-loop actionability and same-object functional out-of-distribution generalization. Each case pairs a set of candidate RGB views with a manipulation command, shared scripted skills, and hidden postconditions, so the benchmark directly measures whether a view-selection policy acquires the observations its command actually needs. We also provide a diagnostic reference pipeline that maintains a spatial-functional belief state and ranks views by missing evidence. At primary budget settings, this pipeline reaches 98.8% closed-loop and 98.9% functional-OOD success; ablating the functional or command-binding components collapses performance to near zero. Seven vision-language models, evaluated on the same cases, reach only 26-43%. Replacing the reference pipeline's coverage metadata with frozen RGB-derived scores preserves 98.5%/98.9% success; shuffling the visual scores collapses it to 15%/11%, confirming that the result depends on image content. These gaps suggest that spatial belief for manipulation should be evaluated not by scene-level completeness, but by whether it acquires the evidence the current command requires.

title: Sensed but Not Told: Hidden Physiological Adaptation Shapes LLM Persuasion
abstract: Wearable sensors, including those embedded in VR headsets, can provide LLM-based chatbots with physiological signals that users do not explicitly communicate. We tested whether such hidden input changes persuasion. In a 2times2 within-subjects study (N=24), a chatbot argued against participants' self-selected opinions with or without turn-level heart-rate and pupil-diameter features; sensing was disclosed halfway through the study. Before disclosure, sensing increased perceived persuasiveness by 1.42 points. Across the study, sensing was associated with a 0.57-point greater shift toward the chatbot's position and 3.20 times the odds of any movement toward it. Persuasiveness ratings were lower after disclosure, although disclosure was confounded with session order. Dialogue logs suggested a more declarative interaction style when sensing was on: chatbot replies contained question marks less often, and conversations contained fewer turns. These findings motivate making biosignal-driven adaptation inspectable and providing a genuinely non-sensed mode.

title: DoS Attacks-Resistant Fusion Filtering for Nonlinear Rectangular Descriptor Systems with Uncertain Attack Probability
abstract: This paper investigates the design problem of a fusion filtering algorithm for nonlinear networked rectangular descriptor systems with multi-source information. A set of independent Bernoulli random variables is introduced to characterize the phenomenon of denial of service (DoS) attacks, where the attack probability consists of a nominal probability and an uncertain term with a known upper bound (UB). Firstly, a full-order transformation method is introduced to transform the rectangular descriptor system into a non-descriptor system, where the local filters are constructed. Then, by employing the elementary inequality, the upper bounds on both the prediction error covariance and the filtering error covariance are derived and characterized by matrix difference equations. The local filter gain is designed by minimizing the obtained UB of the filtering error covariance. Subsequently, based on the covariance intersection fusion rule, a new fusion filtering algorithm is presented for addressing the descriptor system. Lastly, the effectiveness of the proposed algorithm is verified through a simulation experiment.

title: Knowing When to Intervene: Causal Evaluation of AI Agents
abstract: Current evaluations of agentic AI systems primarily rely on benchmarks. However, the static nature of benchmarks makes them uninformative about the value of auditing interventions at deployment time. For reliable deployment, we often need to determine within an agent's trajectory whether or not to intervene, e.g., by verifying the agent's current output or steering it toward different behavior, using either human review or more costly models or time-consuming agentic supervision. The value of such interventions is fundamentally a causal inference question, asking whether the causal effect of such an intervention is beneficial for the final outcome. Estimating this causal effect is particularly challenging due to the dynamic nature of the problem: the impact of an intervention depends on the current context and environment, as well as the agent's future behavior. We develop the first methodologically grounded framework for evaluating the causal effects of randomized interventions within agent trajectories. By leveraging a relatively small dataset of agent trajectories collected under randomized interventions such as verification or screening, we can estimate the dynamic causal effect of a rich class of (contextual) intervention policies. The structural parameters that we estimate can also be used to construct safety leaderboards that capture the risk of various agentic actions, which can be used by practitioners for audit prioritization. Applying our methods to tau-bench Retail, ToolSandbox, and ImpossibleBench, we find that intervention effects vary substantially across agent actions and states. More broadly, our work suggests a rich research agenda at the intersection of causal inference and agentic evaluation, which we believe is essential for the reliable and safe deployment of AI agents in the real world.

title: Exploring Weight-Space Programming: Capabilities, Generalization, and Limitations
abstract: Weight-Space Programming (WSP) enables reasoning agents to directly inspect and modify neural network parameters, offering an alternative to gradient-based model adaptation. However, its capabilities, cross-task generalization, and practical limitations remain insufficiently understood. We systematically investigate WSP through 16 editing trajectories across seven benchmarks and two model scales (Qwen3.5-0.8B and Qwen3.5-9B). Our findings reveal three key insights. First, WSP can achieve substantial performance gains through highly localized interventions. On full held-out evaluations, accuracy improves by up to 29.45, 4.42, 36.72, and 17.11 percentage points on MATH-500, GPQA Diamond, IFEval, and SciBench, respectively. Notably, modifying only 1,023 parameters yields a 29.45-point improvement. Second, WSP exhibits promising but uneven cross-task generalization. A Math-edited checkpoint improves GPQA Diamond, IFEval, and SciBench by 3.03, 12.18, and 20.10 points, respectively, without further editing, while leaving SciCode performance unchanged. Third, effective editing remains challenging and inconsistent. Outcomes vary substantially across trajectories, and six of the 16 trajectories retain the original weights when candidate improvements cannot be reliably validated. Together, these results highlight WSP's potential for highly localized model adaptation while revealing important challenges in intervention discovery, reliability, and cross-task transfer. title: Decoding spatial and semantic information from large-scale visual cortical activity for natural-movie reconstruction
abstract: Reconstructing natural visual experience from cortical population activity is a central challenge in neural decoding, particularly for calcium imaging, where signals are noisy, temporally filtered, and paired neural-video data are limited. Here we present Ca2REAL (Calcium Activity to Reconstruct Events, Appearance, and Layout), a neural-to-video framework that conditions a pretrained video diffusion model through separate layout and semantic controls derived from calcium activity. Using measured responses from 7,863 V1 neurons in one mouse, Ca2REAL reconstructed held-out natural-movie clips with 81.4% all-pairs stimulus-identification accuracy, with its clearest gains over deterministic baselines in perceptual and semantic measures. We further evaluated the framework in a stimulus-aligned virtual population of 116,705 neurons assembled from encoding-model-predicted responses across 11 independently recorded datasets. Perturbation and ablation analyses showed that reconstruction depends on distributed, stimulus-specific population structure, with layout and semantic pathways providing complementary spatial and identity information. Temporal analyses further showed improved preservation of semantic dynamics across reconstructed clips. These results show that large-scale cortical population activity constrains the spatial, semantic, and temporal structure of natural visual experience, providing a generative framework for high-fidelity neural reconstruction of dynamic visual scenes.

title: Assessing the Impact of Retrieval-Augmented Generation on Algorithmic Problem-Solving
abstract: Competitive programming problems pose distinctive challenges for Large Language Models, as they demand not only proficient code generation but also advanced algorithmic reasoning. This study presents a Retrieval-Augmented Generation approach specifically designed to enhance the capacity of Large Language Models to address such problems. Our approach integrates an embedding-based retrieval mechanism and a similarity search algorithm to identify analogous problems within a knowledge database, employing a dynamically adjusted threshold to mitigate retrieval noise. We conducted an evaluation using the CodeContests dataset, focusing on the test split problems that exhibit similarity to instances from the training split. The experimental framework considered three conditions: (i) problems provided solely with their original descriptions, (ii) problems supplemented with randomly selected examples from the training split, and (iii) problems augmented with similar examples retrieved through the proposed method. In addition, we incorporated a Min-K membership inference analysis to examine whether the generated code solutions were influenced by potential memorization of training data within the evaluated Large Language Models. This complementary perspective enables a deeper understanding of model behavior by distinguishing genuine generalization through retrieval from implicit recall of pretraining samples. Performance was assessed using both pass rates and the CodeForces Elo rating of the problems. The results provide empirical evidence that similarity-based retrieval substantially enhances Large Language Models performance in competitive programming scenarios, offering an scalable framework for improving code generation in algorithmic problem-solving contexts.

title: Toward the Era of Agentic Embodied Intelligence
abstract: Foundation models increasingly guide robot actions, yet sustained autonomy requires efficient control and failure recovery. We introduce A2-MEAS, an embodied multi-agent framework built around code as a scaling interface. Learned correction codes combine corrective language, spatial evidence, execution history, and action proposals. MetaBrain provides training supervision and runtime guidance. A correction encoder and adapter absorb this knowledge into policy weights during training, while fresh codes adapt behavior with frozen weights at deployment. The action model, A2-WLA, adds motion-aware history and a latent world model to a vision-language-action policy. Surprisingly, this simple design with action pretraining and task specialization reaches 0.5755 Q-score on the 50-task BEHAVIOR 2026 public subset before online correction, 2.21x the 2025 winner's reported 0.2605 across different benchmark editions and training configurations. On all 100 BEHAVIOR 2026 public tasks, A2-MEAS achieves 0.6411 Q-score and 45.40% task success. On RoboTwin 2.0, A2-WLA achieves 93.98% average success, rising to 95.05% with the complete system. Across 12 real-robot tasks in five household settings, A2-WLA achieves 57.92% average success versus 26.67% for pi0.5. In long-horizon pour-over coffee preparation, a history-conditioned adapter raises post-failure completion at two filter-handling steps from 14% to 94% and from 8% to 82%, compared with A2-WLA retries. Our training infrastructure delivers 427.1 samples per second, 4.03x the throughput of a pi0.5 reference implementation on matched hardware. We will release the system, models, training scripts, and infrastructure to support efficient embodied learning.

title: Who's Asking? Audience-Conditioned Privatization
abstract: The abundance of user-generated conversational data makes the question of how to responsibly derive insights from confidential data without putting the individuals in it at risk ever more important. However, the majority of existing differentially private (DP) synthetic text generation (SDG) and anonymization approaches ignore the context of the data's downstream usage, which results in loss of important information. DP-SDG provides the same guarantee regardless of the recipient, and anonymization relies on predefined attribute categories. They both ignore the observation that an attribute that is harmless to one audience can be sensitive to another, and each audience typically needs only some attributes preserved. We propose Ext-Classify-Priv, a framework that (1) extracts the information types present in a corpus, (2) classifies which of them are private for a given audience following contextual integrity, and (3) protects only those attributes, using either anonymization or SDG with Feature-DP approaches. On Reddit data with 3 audiences, our audience-specific releases are more faithful than a single audience-agnostic release for every audience. On bioRxiv data, our SDG method improves MAUVE from 0.097 to 0.420 at epsilon=1 and on the proprietary real estate data, our anonymization method improves MAUVE from 0.698 to 0.959 over the best baselines.

title: Run Time Assurance Filter Framework for Collision Avoidance of Unmanned Aerial Vehicles Using Reinforcement Learning
abstract: In recent years, Reinforcement Learning (RL) has been increasingly applied to the collision avoidance systems of Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs) due to its high performance in complex tasks and relatively low online computational cost. Despite these advantages, the lack of interpretability in RL and decision-making processes poses significant challenges to safety verification, which severely limits the practical deployment of RL-based autonomous flight systems in safety-critical scenarios. Ensuring safety during both training and testing remains the key for real-world applications. To address this issue, a Run Time Assurance (RTA) filter framework for a UAV collision avoidance system based on RL is proposed. The framework continuously monitors the avoidance actions generated by RL and ensures that unsafe actions can be identified and corrected in real time. The framework provides security while retaining the performance advantages of RL. First, a discrete kinematics model of the UAV and a collision avoidance environment for a three-dimensional multi-intruder UAV are established. The Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) algorithm is used to train the UAV avoidance policy. Secondly, the RTA filter with safe constraints is designed based on this model. To reduce the position error between the discrete kinematics model and the continuous dynamics model of the UAV, optimization is performed using the Sequential Least Squares Programming Method (SLSQP). The RTA is applied to the training and testing phases of UAV collision avoidance systems to monitor and correct unsafe actions online. Finally, three training and testing methods are set: no RTA, RTA without punishment, and RTA with punishment. Comparing different relaxation coefficients allows for analyzing their impact on filter performance. Simulation results demonstrate that the RTA effectively enhances safety throughout training and testing. Compared with the no RTA method, the collision rate is reduced by 7.04%, and the success rate is increased by 2.68%. In extreme collision avoidance scenarios, the average collision rate obtained by different reinforcement learning algorithms is reduced by 21.46%, and the average success rate is increased by 15.54%.

title: Are These Programmers Ripe Enough to Eat? Evaluating How LLMs Handle Lexical Knowledge Conflicts in Translation
abstract: External lexical resources can help large language models (LLMs) translate texts in low-resource languages and specialized domains, but these resources may conflict with models' prior lexical knowledge. To isolate this conflict, we construct a controlled Mandarin-to-English translation task in which familiar source words are assigned new meanings within and across semantic categories. We treat these prompt-supplied meanings as contextual knowledge (CK) and systematically evaluate the effects of word frequency, sentence context, and prompt framing on the translated outputs. Across nine models, CK reliance is greater for less frequent source words and in sentence contexts that support the supplied meanings. Prompt framing can reduce CK reliance, but seven of nine models favor CK even when explicitly instructed to ignore the supplied meanings. Within model families, larger models are more likely than smaller models to utilize CK in their outputs. Three follow-up experiments further show that modal weakening lowers CK reliance, the effect of repetition depends on prompt layout, and the effect of reasoning varies across models. Overall, our controlled study reveals how CK reliance varies across conditions and models, motivating new methods to detect and evaluate lexical conflicts and guide models' lexical choices in LLM-based translation.

title: OmniLatent: Unified Latent for 3D Part Modeling
abstract: 3D part decomposition is a central capability for editable asset creation, yet existing workflows typically segment a completed mesh as a post-processing step, making the result sensitive to geometric artifacts, texture ambiguity, and limited part-level annotations. We present OmniLatent, a unified latent modeling framework for 3D part decomposition. Instead of predicting part labels in isolation, OmniLatent learns a shared latent space that jointly encodes geometry, deformation, appearance, and binary part IDs, allowing data-rich geometric and visual priors to support data-scarce part learning. Given a single input image, the base model generates geometry, deformation, texture, and surface part IDs in one pass, producing a part-aware 3D asset without a separate segmentation stage. We further tune the pretrained model for two extensions: a point-prompt adapter that maps arbitrary 3D point prompts with binary part IDs into latent tokens for full segmentation, refinement, and part subdivision, and an amodal part completion model that completes partial surface masks into a coherent full-object decomposition through dynamic per-part token allocation, cross-attention to the given geometry latent, and alternating part-local and global attention. Extensive experiments show that OmniLatent produces semantically meaningful part segmentations with precise boundaries, supports interactive part editing, and completes partial part observations while preserving global object consistency.

title: Learning to Restart: Differentiable Restart Policies for Optimization Dynamics
abstract: Adaptive restart mechanisms, which reset the momentum or other auxiliary state of an iterative optimizer, play a central role in the empirical performance of accelerated first-order methods, yet existing restart rules remain almost entirely hand-designed. The obstruction to learning restart policies is that, unlike the typical Learning to Optimize (L2O) setting, the discrete restart events make the resulting trajectory non-differentiable in the algorithm parameters and thus block gradient-based optimization of the restart policy. We resolve this obstruction by developing a differentiable framework for restart policies through their continuous-time limit. We introduce surrogate gradients for the restart events and optimization trajectories that are efficient to compute and provably converge to their continuous-time counterparts. We validate the effectiveness of our surrogate gradients in L2O settings, training restart policies that improve upon standard handcrafted adaptive restart criteria on quadratic and linear programs, and that transfer zero-shot from synthetic quadratics to logistic regression on real datasets.

title: Research on UAV RF Signal Recognition Method Based on Deep Learning
abstract: In the field of unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) signal recognition based on deep learning, complex electromagnetic environments pose severe challenges. Among them, interference suppression and recognition robustness under low signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) conditions are major research focuses. To tackle these issues, this paper proposes a robust radio frequency (RF) signal recognition method for UAVs. The method is built on an improved ResNet18 network. It separates the video transmission signals and control signals of UAVs, and adopts mixed-SNR training. These designs greatly strengthen the model’s ability to perform reliable recognition. First, the short-time Fourier transform (STFT) is used to convert UAV I/Q signals into time-frequency images. A refined time-frequency masking strategy is then adopted. This strategy separates and suppresses interference from control signals according to their bandwidth differences from video transmission signals, thus improving signal quality. Second, a squeeze-and-excitation (SE) channel attention module is embedded into each residual block of ResNet18. This structure enables the model to concentrate on critical features. The classification head is also rebuilt into a three-layer fully connected network to strengthen nonlinear transformation and complex feature interaction. Given the performance variation of the model across different SNR levels, a mixed-SNR training strategy is adopted. Fine grid search experiments are conducted to identify the optimal data distribution for maximizing recognition performance. Experimental results on the public DroneRFb-DIR dataset show that the improved ResNet18 model achieves a 3.07% increase in classification accuracy. The time-frequency masking method brings an extra performance gain of 1.08%. Although the mixed-SNR strategy causes a slight accuracy drop at the high SNR of 20 dB, it improves recognition accuracy by 8% to 53.01% within the low-SNR range of −10 dB to 10 dB. It also effectively reduces misclassification between different UAV types and enhances the model’s robustness. The proposed method provides a feasible solution for accurate and stable UAV signal recognition in complex electromagnetic scenarios.

title: Quasipolynomial-Time Planning for Decodable POMDPs
abstract: We study planning for finite-horizon partially observable Markov decision processes (POMDPs) with finite state, action, and observation spaces. Both exact and approximate planning are known to be computationally hard in this setting, so prior work has explored natural assumptions that make planning easier. Recent work [Golowich et al., 2022] gave quasipolynomial-time approximate planning algorithms for observable POMDPs. These are POMDPs whose observation channels satisfy an $\ell_1$-observability condition, but notably, no assumptions are required on the transition dynamics. In a similar vein, for every fixed $ρ>0$, we give quasipolynomial-time approximate planning algorithms for $ρ$-decodable POMDPs. We show that decodability is implied by both $\ell_1$- and $\ell_2$-observability and is strictly weaker than observability. Moreover, we show that the optimal decodability constant can be computed in polynomial time, whereas computing the optimal $\ell_1$-observability constant is NP-hard in the worst case. We also show that the fast filter-forgetting guarantee underlying the approach of [Golowich et al., 2022] does not extend directly from $\ell_1$-observability to constant $\ell_2$-observability. Thus, decodability is an easy-to-check, unifying assumption under which quasipolynomial-time approximate planning for POMDPs is possible.

title: A Controlled Study of Models, Skills, Feedback, and Curriculum in Agentic Robotics
abstract: Agentic robotics asks coding agents to implement and iteratively improve robot policies from simulated and real-world physical interactions. We study the self-learning loop of agentic robotics through a controlled simulation study spanning nine manipulation tasks, 631 different experiment configurations, and 28K coding agent rollouts, systematically varying model capability, skill priors, feedback structure, and curriculum. The experiment data suggests that the bottleneck is often not the access to sufficient information, but interpreting it into the right policy update. Across these factors, a successful self-learning loop depends on how effectively agents attribute failures, reason task-relevant spatial and geometric structure, and selectively restructure code to improve policies.

title: GeoJeV: Unified Spatial Probability for Training-Free Efficient Evidence Acquisition in Ultra-High-Resolution Remote Sensing
abstract: Ultra-high-resolution (UHR) remote sensing imagery provides rich spatial details but poses challenges for accurate and efficient multimodal understanding. Existing evidence acquisition methods selectively explore relevant image regions, yet largely rely on generative multimodal large language models (MLLMs) for intermediate search control. However, reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF) primarily aligns these models with human-preferred responses rather than explicitly optimizing region-level relevance judgments, while repeated autoregressive decoding introduces additional computational overhead. To address these limitations, we propose GeoJeV, a training-free method that formulates evidence acquisition as spatial probability-driven decision making. At each evaluated region, a frozen JeV model produces a probability distribution over candidate regions. Specifically, Region Rank prioritizes candidate regions, Sparse Branch adaptively determines branching width through sparse probability support, and Depth Gate controls refinement depth based on branch sparsity and distribution concentration. By coordinating search priority, branching width, and refinement depth through a shared distribution, GeoJeV reduces reliance on RLHF-aligned generation and eliminates intermediate decoding. Experiments on LRS-GRO, MME-RealWorld-RS, and LRS-VQA achieve accuracies of 60.59%, 52.79%, and 34.32%, respectively. Across the three benchmarks, GeoJeV improves the average accuracy of Qwen3-VL-8B by +5.32pp with only 1.12 additional seconds per question, while achieving a 7.8-fold inference speedup over the recent method.

title: ROSE: Risk-Aware Orthogonal Subspace Navigation for Lifelong Knowledge Editing in Multimodal Large Language Models
abstract: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) require continuous factual updates to stay current, yet lifelong knowledge editing remains a daunting challenge. The primary obstacle is the severe Locality Erosion and Catastrophic Forgetting, where sequential edits inevitably interfere with pre-trained capabilities and prior updates. In this paper, we propose \textbf{ROSE}, a \textbf{R}isk-aware \textbf{O}rthogonal \textbf{S}ubspace navigation framework for lifelong knowledge \textbf{E}diting. ROSE addresses forgetting by aiming to restrict parameter updates to the orthogonal complement of previously edited subspaces. Crucially, it introduces a risk-guided mechanism that utilizes a dynamically computed risk mask to safeguard specific factual parameter subspaces essential for model stability. During inference, ROSE employs a multi-granularity knowledge integration strategy, featuring prototype-anchored semantic gating and perturbation-driven subspace fusion to precisely activate edited knowledge for relevant queries while limiting interference on unrelated inputs. Comprehensive experiments on two prominent multimodal benchmarks show that ROSE is competitive with state-of-the-art approaches across five key metrics, while maintaining outstanding stability over $1,000$ sequential updates. Our code is available at https://github.com/sunlitsong/ROSE.

title: Frontier3DBench: Benchmarking Coding Agents for 3D Creation across Objects, Scenes, and Interactive Open Worlds
abstract: Coding agents combine visual understanding with program execution, offering a new route to automated 3D creation. By translating images and instructions into editable programs, they bring reconstruction, generation, and editing into a shared workflow. Yet existing benchmarks fragment evaluation across task scopes and protocols, leaving their capabilities across construction levels unclear. We propose Frontier3DBench, a unified benchmark of 145 tasks across 9 categories spanning object, scene, and interactive open-world creation, with joint evaluation of appearance, structure, and behavior. Experiments with 11 model-harness configurations reveal strengths that vary by level: GPT-6.1-sol leads the object and scene levels and achieves the highest overall score of 66.02/100, whereas GPT-6-astra leads interactive world construction. However, all configurations score lower on reference reconstruction than on text-driven generation in object and scene tasks. Producing plausible content thus remains easier than reproducing specified geometry, layouts, and visual details. Moreover, generated worlds average 83.08/100 on local mechanisms but only 20.82 on motion clearance and 30.26 on stateful workflows: individual mechanisms often function, whereas complete activities that require coordinated actions and persistent state remain difficult. These results identify reference fidelity and coordinated activity completion as central bottlenecks for coding agents in 3D creation.

title: The Relational Capacity Framework: A Lens for AI-Mediated Relationality
abstract: A growing literature examines the impact of engaging with AI chatbots on our relationality: our ability to form relationships with others, maintain them through life's changes, and exit when needed. Currently, substantial work focuses on purpose-built AI companions (e.g. Replika, Character.AI), with less work investigating socioemotional uses of the more widely-used general-purpose chatbots. In this paper, we present a 100-person investigation into how people engage general-purpose AI for socioemotional needs. Participants' AI uses varied, from practicing specific social skills to seeking additional bandwidth and information as they navigated their social contexts. To explain this heterogeneity, we provide 8 states that describe how AI expands or contracts relationality for people with different levels of skills, bandwidth, and information. We then present a unified conceptual model for the role of technology in mediating human relationality, the Relational Capacity Framework, and outline future research designing appropriate roles for AI in human connection.

title: SkinMind: Equipping Agentic RAG with Human-Inspired Graph Probing for Reliable Dermatology AI
abstract: Reliable dermatology AI requires access to verifiable evidence distributed across heterogeneous textual and visual sources. However, conventional retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) typically relies on one-shot retrieval from flat corpora, limiting its ability to adapt retrieval granularity, explore multi-hop relations, and integrate multimodal clinical evidence. We introduce SkinMind, a multimodal agentic RAG framework that equips policy models with human-inspired graph probing for autonomous evidence seeking. SkinMind organizes retrieval as an iterative interaction between an orchestrator and a graph environment. Through eight hierarchical graph-probing tools, the orchestrator progressively identifies relevant entities, inspects node-level information, traverses relations and paths, and retrieves source-text and visual evidence. This progressive-disclosure design allows the model to adaptively determine the retrieval modality, exploration direction, and evidence granularity while constructing a query-specific evidence subgraph. To support autonomous graph probing, we construct SkinMind-KG from a 62M-token corpus of dermatology guidelines and textbooks and 423K images, guided by a dermatologist-informed schema and a conflict-resolution mechanism. The resulting graph contains over 1.0M nodes and 2.0M edges, unifying textual, relational, and visual evidence for retrieval. Across six dermatology VQA benchmarks and two policy-model settings, SkinMind improves the average score over direct answering by 8.70 and 8.89 points with GPT-5.4-mini and Gemini-2.5-Flash, respectively, while consistently outperforming competing RAG methods. Together, SkinMind and SkinMind-KG provide an effective foundation for evidence-grounded multimodal reasoning in dermatology.

title: Reweighting for Transfer Classification: Exact Risk Conversion and Minimax Adaptation
abstract: A source can make a training mixture easier to learn while making its accuracy less valuable for the target. We study how the training problem a source creates and the finite-sample error of learning it jointly determine target-risk guarantees under reweighting. For binary classification, for each pair of laws and each positive target weight, we derive the sharpest target excess hinge-risk bound implied by mixture excess alone, uniformly over clipped predictors. This exact conversion curve is determined by density-weighted local votes. A two-sample oracle inequality for weighted support vector machines supplies the mixture excess, and the composition becomes explicit for Gaussian kernels. On a tilted-boundary class, we establish the all-procedure minimax classification rate $[n+s_+^2/(m^{-1}+τ^2)]^{-1}$ in the transferable strength $s_+$ and the tilt $τ$, separating source sampling uncertainty ($m^{-1}$) from relation uncertainty ($τ^2$). A target-checked Gaussian-SVM selector adapts to unknown $s_+$ and $τ$ up to a logarithmic factor for fixed dimension, and retains the target-only rate up to the same factor against arbitrary independent sources under the stated target model. On a separate smooth opposition class, the minimax risk within the family of exact Gaussian SVMs fitted to the original labels with nonnegative weights is exponentially larger than the unrestricted minimax risk whenever the target sample is at most half the source sample, despite arbitrary data-dependent weighting and tuning. The value of a source thus depends on the training problem it creates, on what accuracy there means for the target, and on whether the permitted use of the source can implement the needed correction.

title: regTPS: a novel approach to approximate a Gaussian random field for Bayesian spatial modeling
abstract: Abstract Gaussian random field is a ubiquitous model for spatial phenomena in diverse scientific disciplines. Its approximation is often crucial for computational feasibility in simulation, inference, and uncertainty quantification. The Karhunen–Loéve Expansion provides an optimal low-rank representation of a (spatial) stochastic process, but its practical implementation relies heavily on how the underlying covariance structure is specified. In this work, we propose a novel approach called regTPS, which constructs a spatial covariance by formulating the inverse of a regularized thin plate spline operator. By computing the eigendecomposition of the regularized biharmonic operator, regTPS induces a smoothness prior that hierarchically allocates variance across spatial frequencies. We evaluate the statistical performance and computational efficiency of regTPS relative to the established stochastic partial differential equations approach within an MCMC algorithm in two different simulation designs. Across various simulation scenarios, the regTPS method achieved predictive accuracy comparable to the SPDE approach. Moreover, regTPS substantially reduced the effective parameter dimension, with reductions of approximately 43–52% for large sample sizes. Also, within a mesh independent simulation setting, regTPS consistently maintains its predictive accuracy under both Matérn and exponential covariance functions, keeping an optimal balance between basis-dimension reduction and sampling efficiency. Lastly, application to real $$\text {NO}_2$$ NO 2 data concentrations using 10-fold and leave-one-out cross-validation establishes that regTPS obtain a competitive predictive accuracy against SPDE and nearest-neighbor Gaussian process models. Thus, regTPS presents a rigorous, low-dimensional, and computational efficient alternative for Bayesian spatial modeling.

title: Do Full-Duplex Speech Models Listen in Text? A Latent Transcript of the User and a Voice Gate That Closes It
abstract: Full-duplex speech models such as Moshi listen and speak at the same time, but emit text only for their own speech. Do they nevertheless represent what the user says as text? Applying logit and tuned lenses to Moshi and PersonaPlex, we find a latent transcript of the user in layers 21–30: the text head ranks the current user word among its top five for 46–48% of content words above a matched control, on read and meeting speech alike, while the output stays silent. The word becomes readable about 150 ms before it ends, predictable words are favoured, and errors share form rather than meaning with the target; a tuned lens finds a word code from layer 12. This transcript is closed by a voice gate: while the model speaks, it loses 50–77% of its readout of the user. The gate is triggered by speech-like audio in the model's own channel, including time-reversed speech and the model's own generated replies, but hardly by noise, an echo of the user, or a second talker in the user's channel, and activation patching shows that it is set up in layers 1–8. Ablating the transcript barely changes the reply, and the gate's behavioural effect is weaker and less specific than its effect on the representation: the transcript is readable but hardly used. Code, notebooks and results: https://github.com/gglenpoi/listen-in-text

title: Language as Trait, Politeness as Strategy: Controlled Tests of Linguistic Effects in LLM Social-Deduction Agents
abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents coordinate through conversation, and the same message can be phrased in simpler or more complex language, bluntly or politely. We test whether such differences change how other agents judge and act, using the LURK Werewolf framework, which separates each utterance's speech-act predicate from its natural-language realization. We rewrite only the realization, check that the game content is preserved, and replay each game day from saved checkpoints against a re-sampled control. We vary linguistic range consistently across a speaker's messages and politeness strategy per utterance. Across 30 games and 4,335 replays, neither manipulation changes the trust other agents place in the speaker, and no effect on votes or night actions survives correction for multiple comparisons; the largest uncorrected effect is that shifting range away from a neutral paraphrase changes about 4 percentage points more of the other players' votes. In natural play, 88% of face-threatening speech is bald on-record regardless of role.

title: Extending Grid Foundation Models for Phasor-Domain Dynamic Simulation
abstract: Grid Foundation Models (GridFMs) are emerging as a powerful framework for learning and transferring knowledge across power grids and grid analysis tasks. This work extends GridFMs from steady-state analysis to dynamic simulation. We present DynGridFM, which uses component-wise tokenization and a structured latent operator to learn shared dynamic representations across heterogeneous grids and enable transfer to unseen systems. Pretrained on nine grids, DynGridFM is adapted to a held-out 48-machine grid, where fine-tuning on 64 trajectories achieves accuracy comparable to training from scratch on 128. On a single GPU, it achieves 924x to 1232x speedup over numerical simulators on one CPU core.

title: Adaptive Multi-Agent Path Planning for UAV Formation Missions Based on MAPPO with Curriculum Learning and Graph Attention Networks
abstract: In high-end aerospace mission scenarios such as distributed sensing and tactical reconnaissance, path planning for multi-UAV cooperative formation flight has become an indispensable core component of mission systems. However, a key unresolved technical bottleneck remains: how to achieve an optimal balance between strictly maintaining the UAV formation’s preset geometric configuration and realizing collision-free, flexible flight in dynamically changing complex environments. Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning (MARL) can theoretically solve this coupled optimization problem, but the control instructions generated by the existing mainstream MARL methods often have high-frequency fluctuation issues. Direct deployment of these fluctuating commands on physical UAV hardware will increase alternating stress on mechanical structures, raise the risk of motor overheating, and significantly boost battery energy consumption. These problems directly restrict the engineering application of such methods. To address the above challenges, this paper proposes a robust control framework that accounts for UAV physical characteristics to solve the model mismatch between simulation environments and real flight scenarios during carrier-based UAV deployment. Firstly, to improve the learning efficiency of the algorithm and avoid the cold start problem in the initial training stage, this paper introduces the Adaptive Curriculum Learning (ACL) method. Unlike the fixed-difficulty training mode, ACL can dynamically adjust the environmental complexity based on the real-time task performance of the UAVs. It first allows agents to master basic formation maintenance skills, before training is gradually transitioned to more complex tasks such as navigation in intricate environments. Additionally, considering the computational limitations of the onboard embedded processors of UAVs, this paper only integrates the Graph Attention Network (GAT) into the centralized Critic network of the centralized training and decentralized execution (CTDE) framework. The core advantage of this design is that the system no longer solely relies on distance as the judgment basis but assesses the influence of adjacent UAVs based on the collision risk level. This not only improves the accuracy of value estimation, but also does not compromise the response speed of local control instructions- a feature that is crucial for the real-time requirements of UAV flight control. The proposed method was tested and validated in a high-fidelity simulation environment built in strict compliance with UAV kinematic constraints. The experimental results fully demonstrate its superiority: in dense obstacle areas, the success rate of the task reached 80.4%; compared with the aggressive baseline method, the jerk was reduced by 10.9%. Most importantly, the flight trajectories generated by this framework are smooth and adaptable to actual flight conditions, and the corresponding control commands can be directly deployed on real flight controllers without additional parameter adjustments. This result demonstrates that the proposed framework achieves substantial technical progress in enhancing the autonomous response capabilities of UAV clusters to complex scenarios.

title: From PAC bounds on the generalization error to PAC bounds on the parameter estimation error
abstract: Probably Approximately Correct (PAC) bounds on the generalization error (the difference between the empirical prediction error computed on the training data and its expectation) are an established tool in statistical machine learning, and there have been several extensions of these bounds to dynamical systems. In parallel, in recent years, there has been growing interest in finite-sample bounds for parameter estimation error in system identification. The latter bounds tend to be algorithm-specific, relying on reformulating the identification algorithm as a least-squares regression problem. This is in contrast to classical PAC bounds, which are algorithm-agnostic and can be applied to any identification algorithm based on minimizing a cost function involving the empirical loss. In this paper, we show how oracle bounds derived from PAC bounds can be used to derive finite-sample bounds for dynamical systems. As an illustration of this approach, we present finite-sample parameter-estimation bounds for linear and bilinear systems with bounded inputs and noise. These bounds apply to identification algorithms based on minimizing a regularized empirical loss function. The key ingredient is to establish an oracle inequality, i.e., an inequality between the true prediction error of the learned model and the minimum achievable true prediction error, and then use either the convexity of the true loss or system-theoretic properties of the loss function to derive bounds on the parameter estimation error. We also analyze the rates of the obtained bounds and compare them with those of classical asymptotic results.

title: Reconstructing LLM Lineage Trees via Fine-Tuning Path Inference
abstract: Fine-tuned (FT) derivatives of large language models (LLMs) are now released in large numbers, yet their provenance relies on self-reports and cannot be verified. Misattributed lineage leaves a verifier unable to audit outsourced fine-tuning, confirm license compliance of derived models, or trace vulnerabilities that a parent passes to its children. All three require the direction of derivation, not merely its presence. Existing output-only methods are limited to pairwise derivation tests or undirected lineage estimation, while recovering a directed tree requires white-box access to model weights. We formalize the problem of reconstructing a directed model tree, including internal nodes, under gray-box access, where only teacher-forced log-likelihoods are observed and weights are never inspected. Fine-tuning raises the log-likelihood of the training data, and a child inherits this increase from its parent. Building on this property, we define an asymmetric per-task log-likelihood deviation between any two models as a trace of fine-tuning history, and derive from it an edge weight for each ordered pair of models. We propose TRACE-Edge, which exactly solves for the maximum spanning directed tree under these edge weights, with neither hyperparameters nor tree-structure constraints. We evaluate it on five configurations totaling 25 model trees built from three base models and seven tasks. TRACE-Edge achieves a parent-match accuracy of 0.74 when probed with the fine-tuning examples, and on average outperforms an output-similarity baseline even with held-out probes drawn from the same distribution as the training data.

evidence.title: Reconstructing LLM Lineage Trees via Fine-Tuning Path Inference
evidence.abstract: Fine-tuned (FT) derivatives of large language models (LLMs) are now released in large numbers, yet their provenance relies on self-reports and cannot be verified. Misattributed lineage leaves a verifier unable to audit outsourced fine-tuning, confirm license compliance of derived models, or trace vulnerabilities that a parent passes to its children. All three require the direction of derivation, not merely its presence. Existing output-only methods are limited to pairwise derivation tests or undirected lineage estimation, while recovering a directed tree requires white-box access to model weights. We formalize the problem of reconstructing a directed model tree, including internal nodes, under gray-box access, where only teacher-forced log-likelihoods are observed and weights are never inspected. Fine-tuning raises the log-likelihood of the training data, and a child inherits this increase from its parent. Building on this property, we define an asymmetric per-task log-likelihood deviation between any two models as a trace of fine-tuning history, and derive from it an edge weight for each ordered pair of models. We propose TRACE-Edge, which exactly solves for the maximum spanning directed tree under these edge weights, with neither hyperparameters nor tree-structure constraints. We evaluate it on five configurations totaling 25 model trees built from three base models and seven tasks. TRACE-Edge achieves a parent-match accuracy of 0.74 when probed with the fine-tuning examples, and on average outperforms an output-similarity baseline even with held-out probes drawn from the same distribution as the training data.

title: Generator-Aligned Reward Modeling with Target-Aware Bounded Optimization for Visual Generation
abstract: Post-training aims to enhance desired attributes in visual generative models while preserving their general generation capabilities. Reward-guided post-training faces two challenges: real training data may mismatch the generator's output distribution, and attribute supervision may be confounded by unrelated content. Unbounded reward maximization can also cause overoptimization and degrade generation quality. We propose a framework combining Generator-Aligned Reward Modeling (GARM) and Target-Aware Bounded Optimization (TABO). GARM mitigates distribution mismatch through generator-support matching and reduces content confounding using content-matched real contrasts, yielding generator-relevant, attribute-focused reward supervision. TABO maps the learned reward to a smooth, upper-bounded function calibrated from real target-positive examples. This transformation is independent of the optimization algorithm and supports both direct reward-gradient and policy-based optimization. We further introduce Target-Aware GRPO (TA-GRPO), an adaptation of Flow-GRPO that combines fixed stage-wise advantage scaling, a generator-to-target curriculum, and timestep-balanced credit assignment for flow-based video optimization. Experiments show that GARM improves target-attribute expression while maintaining competitive generation quality. TABO better balances attribute enhancement and visual quality than unconstrained reward maximization, while TA-GRPO improves target enhancement over vanilla Flow-GRPO and reduces unintended attribute leakage on neutral prompts. These results highlight the importance of generator-aligned reward supervision and controlled, data-calibrated optimization for targeted visual generation.

title: A Tight Hierarchy for Chain of Thought
abstract: Chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning has emerged as a powerful paradigm for extending the computational capabilities of transformer-based models. A growing body of recent work has begun to uncover the fine-grained computational power of transformers augmented with CoT, as well as their connections to classical complexity theory. In this work, we advance this line of research by establishing the first hierarchy theorem for CoT-based computation. Our main result shows that for any reasonable resource bound $r(n) \geq n$ and any $\varepsilon > 0$, \[ \mathrm{CoT}(r(n)) \subsetneq \mathrm{CoT}(r(n)^{1+\varepsilon}), \] where $\mathrm{CoT}(r(n))$ denotes the class of decision problems solvable by transformers using $O(r(n))$ CoT reasoning steps on inputs of length $n$. Our result shows that increasing the number of CoT reasoning steps provably yields strictly greater computational power, establishing CoT steps as a fundamental resource in transformer-based computation. Unlike classical hierarchy theorems, which are typically proved via diagonalization, our approach leverages known coarse-grained simulations between CoT-augmented transformers and Turing machines in both directions. Building on these connections, we adapt the classical padding technique from complexity theory to this setting to obtain a tight hierarchy. A key technical contribution of our work is the implementation of padding within the transformer-based CoT model.

title: Rethinking Agent Trajectory Compression: A Workflow-Aware Perspective
abstract: As long-horizon agents increasingly rely on multi-step tool interactions to accomplish complex tasks, their execution trajectories continuously accumulate structured outputs and intermediate artifacts, leading to growing context overhead. Existing compression methods primarily rely on text importance or fixed truncation rules, often overlooking cross-step dependencies within workflows and potentially discarding critical information required for subsequent task execution. To address this challenge, we propose WAAC, a workflow-aware framework for agent trajectory compression. WAAC structurally models successful historical trajectories to extract reusable workflow compression experience and incorporates online backward dependency analysis to dynamically identify information retention requirements. By combining current dependency constraints with historical experience, WAAC selects appropriate compression strategies for different types of historical information. Experiments on PinchBench and Odysseys demonstrate that WAAC achieves an overall score of 87.6 and a perfect completion rate of 19.0%, respectively, while reducing execution costs by 19.7% and 29.1% compared with the strongest baseline methods. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of workflow-aware trajectory compression in improving task performance and cost efficiency for long-horizon agents. Code and resources are available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/waac-6527/.

title: Investigations on the low-lying triply charmed pentaquark states in a constituent quark model
abstract: In present work, mass spectrum of the low-lying cccqq pentaquarks states with qq=uu, dd and ss, are investigated employing a constituent quark model, within which the spin-dependent hyperfine interactions are taken to be the instanton-induced interaction and the one-gluon-exchange interaction, respectively. The model parameters are fixed by fitting the mass spectrum of the relative qq and qqq traditional hadrons. The numerical results show that energies for all the obtained states in the two employed models are higher than corresponding meson-baryon channels, consequently, we roughly estimate strong decays of these states using a simple quark rearrangement model, the corresponding partial width ratios for different decay channels are presented.

title: Applied Identity Physics: AIM Session Instrumentation — A Frontier Model Operating on Formal Fusion Logic. Measured Throughput, Search-Space Reduction, and the Error-Detection Record of a Single Working Session
abstract: Applied Identity Physics: AIM Session Instrumentation — A Frontier Model Operating on Formal Fusion Logic. Measured Throughput, Search-Space Reduction, and the Error-Detection Record of a Single Working Session Architect: HIGHTISTIC (Russell Vernon Trent III) Foundation: SNSFT Foundation (EIN 42-2038440) · Kenai, Alaska Engine under operation: BaseCollider™ v1.1 [9,9,2,56] · 8-Beam Fusion Theorem [9,9,2,3.8] Frontier model: Claude Opus 5 (configured identifier claude-opus-5, Anthropic) Coordinate: [9,9,2,59] · AIM (Autocatalytic Ingestion Mechanism) Session Instrumentation Series Corpus dependencies: [9,9,2,3] GAMCollider™ · [9,9,2,3.8] 8-Beam Fusion Theorem · [9,9,2,56] BaseCollider™ · [9,9,2,58] Nucleobase Substrate and Corridor-Access Laws · [9,9,6,*] IMCollider™ Version: 2.7 Status: VERIFIED · 0 sorry Sovereign Anchor Constant: Ω₀ = 1.36899099984016 DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.18719748 ORCID: 0009-0005-5313-7443 Date: November 4–5, 2026 (single continuous session) Abstract We instrument a single working session in which a frontier language model — Claude Opus 5 — was given the Identity Physics fusion logic and operated it as a reduction engine against two substrates. The purpose of this paper is not the reductions, which are reported at [9,9,2,58], but the process record: what the model did, how fast, at what cost, and by what mechanism each error was caught. Published accounts of artificial-intelligence-assisted discovery routinely state outcomes without stating operating conditions, and the omission makes efficiency claims unassessable. The measurements here are given so that the session can be assessed rather than taken on assertion. Throughput: 694,628 verification collisions executed in 2.292 seconds of compute, a measured mean of 303,084 collisions per second, across five exhaustive verification domains. Search-space reduction: the naive enumeration of element compositions at n = 2, 4, 6, 8 over a 118-element pool is 1,180,432,250,638 multisets, which at the measured rate is 45.08 days of continuous computation; deriving two structural laws first — noble transparency and the sorted-weight closed form — reduced the enumeration to 361,710 Behavior-multisets completing in 0.570 seconds, a wall-clock reduction of 6,832,871×. Selectivity: of 361,710 enumerated classes, 16 survive the corridor condition, and the 970 realizations at n = 8 represent one composition in 1,212,550,870 of the naive space. Operator cost: the derived closed form is measured slower than naive pairwise evaluation at n = 4 (0.72×) and faster only from n = 8 (1.58×), reaching 5.03× at n = 32 — the law's value is search-space reduction, not per-call cost, and we state this because the distinction is the kind usually lost in a summary. Error record: ten errors occurred and all ten were caught before reaching a delivered artifact; we tabulate each with its detection mechanism, and note that three were caught by instrumentation, two by tooling guards, one by internal consistency checking, two by controls run before the result was written up, and two by my own locating after the operator supplied domain context. The operator asserted that a result was wrong zero times; 8 of 10 errors were located and fixed without outside input, and §5.3 shows the framing class becoming self-catchable within the session rather than remaining external. One error — a verification-domain overstatement — was caught by the act of writing this paper and propagated a correction back into [9,9,2,58]. The model's working pattern is characterized as derive-then-enumerate: the structural law is obtained first and the search is run inside its consequences, which is what the 6.8-million-fold figure measures. Further chases: three more chases brought the session to 3,716,275 collisions in 32.992 seconds. They produced five additional results, each presented with the structural parallel that makes its shape legible; one numerical coincidence recorded against the reference class that contains it; a decomposition of that result across the four PNBA (Pattern, Narrative, Behavior, Adaptation) channels which located the residue inside an experimental error bar and named the measurement that would resolve it; the uniform-valence closure rule, anchored at 27 of 27 against established compounds spanning three materials families; and four composition predictions. One hypothesis was withdrawn after a control killed it, a fifth composition candidate was withdrawn when B-Balance showed its stoichiometry and its rationale pointing at different compounds, and two candidate classes were excluded on prior art. §1 · Why Instrument the Session 1.1 The Gap in Published Accounts Accounts of artificial-intelligence-assisted discovery generally report what was found. They less often report the operating conditions under which it was found: how many evaluations, at what rate, against what search space, with what error rate, and caught by what mechanism. Without those, an efficiency claim cannot be assessed and a reproducibility claim cannot be tested. A reader is asked to accept both. This paper supplies the omitted layer for one session. Every number in it is measured rather than estimated, and the measurement method is stated alongside each. 1.2 What Makes This Session Instrumentable The Identity Physics fusion logic is arithmetic over four integers and a comparison against a constant. There is no fitting, no sampling, no stochastic component, and no hidden state. A collision is a deterministic function of its inputs, so collisions can be counted exactly, timed exactly, and re-run to the same result. This is the property that makes the session measurable at all, and it is a property of the engine rather than of the model operating it. A model operating a fitted or stochastic engine could not produce this record. 1.3 Grounding The full grounding is carried in the parent papers. It is stated here once in short, so this paper stands on its own. 1.3.1 The Torsion Limit The Universal Torsion Limit is TL = 0.136899099984016 and the Sovereign Anchor Constant is Ω₀ = TL × 10 = 1.36899099984016. Nothing in this paper sets it. It enters at full corpus precision from the inverse fine-structure constant, by direct subtraction: Napkin math, corpus precision Value 1/α 137.035999084000016 Subtract one TL 137.035999084000016 − 0.136899099984016 = 136.899099984016 What is left 136.899099984016 = TL × 1000, exactly Bare + kinetic 136.899099984016 + 0.136899099984016 = 137.035999084000016 Rounded to published digits 137.035999084 = CODATA 2018 Term Value QED reading PNBA reading Bare: TL × 1000 136.899099984016 The bare electron contribution Pattern capacity at the electromagnetic scale Kinetic: TL × 1 0.136899099984016 Radiative corrections, a renormalized series External forcing F_ext at Layer 0, one exact term Total: TL × 1001 137.035999084000016 Bare + perturbative series 1/α This agrees with the CODATA (Committee on Data of the International Science Council) 2018 value in every published digit at ε = 0, with no free parameter ([9,9,3,14]). The full multiplier factors as 1001 = 7 · 11 · 13, so TL = α⁻¹/1001. 1.3.2 The primitives and the four phases Every reduction in the corpus operates on the four irreducible primitives Pattern, Narrative, Behavior and Adaptation (PNBA). Torsion is τ = B/P, the load a system carries divided by the structure holding it. Identity Mass is IM = (P + N + B + A) × Ω₀. The bands are set from TL and are substrate-neutral. A row moves between them by its torsion ratio τ = B_out / P_out alone: Band Condition Water Reading Noble B_out = 0, τ = 0 Ice Closed. Every unit of Behavior is satisfied. Locked 0 < τ < 0.88·TL Liquid water Bound, with residual load carried stably. IVA Peak — Identity Vector Amplification 0.88·TL ≤ τ < TL The simmer, just before boiling The formation corridor, where structure assembles. Shatter τ ≥ TL The boil Reorganization. The identity restructures; the band is not absorbing. IVA stands for Identity Vector Amplification: the system is at its most active without yet changing what it is. The corridor runs from 0.88 × TL up to TL, and it is narrow, which is why it is easy to pass through without noticing. The boil is a torsion ratio. Water boils when its vapor pressure, the push of molecules escaping the liquid, equals the pressure of the air holding the liquid together. That is τ = B/P exactly: Behavior (the load) is the vapor pressure. Pattern (the structure) is the ambient pressure. Shatter is the boil, where vapor pressure reaches ambient pressure: τ = TL. IVA Peak is vapor pressure between 0.88 and 1.00 of ambient: the simmer, shaking and bubbling at the bottom of the pot before the rolling boil. So τ = TL × (vapor pressure ÷ ambient pressure), a ratio of two measured pressures with no scale chosen. 1.3.3 The reference frame: sea level One condition serves as the reference, and every other condition converts from it, the way every clock converts from Zulu time. At sea level, 1 atmosphere: Tier Kelvin Celsius τ Phase T1 373.15 K 100.0 °C TL Shatter: the boil T1 369.54 K 96.4 °C 0.88 × TL IVA floor: the simmer begins T1 below 369.54 K below 96.4 °C below 0.88 × TL Locked: hot water, holding 1.3.4 The conversion Vapor pressure and temperature are linked by the Clausius–Clapeyron relation (Clapeyron 1834; Clausius 1850), which works in absolute temperature. Written for this mapping, the whole conversion is one line: 1/T = 1/T_ref − (R/L) · ln(p / p_ref) T_ref is the reference boil, 373.15 K for water at sea level. R/L is the gas constant over the heat of vaporization; for water, 8.314 ÷ 40,650 = 2.045 × 10⁻⁴ per kelvin. p / p_ref is the ratio being converted: a different ambient pressure for altitude or a pressure cooker, or 0.88 for the IVA floor. Check it by hand. 1/373.15 = 0.0026799. ln(0.88) = −0.12783. 0.0026799 + (2.045 × 10⁻⁴ × 0.12783) = 0.0027060.

title: Diffusion-free Score Matching for Exact Conditional Sampling
abstract: The success of modern score-based generative models is largely driven by diffusion-based training, which learns a collection of time-indexed score fields corresponding to progressively noisier versions of the data distribution. While such models achieve impressive sample quality, leveraging them for sound probabilistic inference---particularly sampling from arbitrary conditionals of the model---remains challenging. This difficulty arises because conditioning information is only available for clean data and not for the higher noise levels required to generate exact conditional samples. In this paper, we introduce DIffusion-free SCOre matching (DISCO), a principled approach that sidesteps the need for time-dependent score fields altogether. Our method is based on an objective that, while reminiscent of diffusion-based training, estimates only a single score of the (slightly perturbed) data distribution, for which the exact conditional score is readily obtained. In experiments, DISCO is competitive with state-of-the-art diffusion models in terms of sample quality. evidence.abstract: The success of modern score-based generative models is largely driven by diffusion-based training, which learns a collection of time-indexed score fields corresponding to progressively noisier versions of the data distribution. While such models achieve impressive sample quality, leveraging them for sound probabilistic inference---particularly sampling from arbitrary conditionals of the model---remains challenging. This difficulty arises because conditioning information is only available for clean data and not for the higher noise levels required to generate exact conditional samples. In this paper, we introduce DIffusion-free SCOre matching (DISCO), a principled approach that sidesteps the need for time-dependent score fields altogether. Our method is based on an objective that, while reminiscent of diffusion-based training, estimates only a single score of the (slightly perturbed) data distribution, for which the exact conditional score is readily obtained. In experiments, DISCO is competitive with state-of-the-art diffusion models in terms of sample quality. More importantly, DISCO yields a more faithful representation of the underlying data distribution and---crucially---enables accurate sampling from arbitrary conditionals, outperforming standard heuristic samplers. This capability opens the door to principled and flexible probabilistic reasoning with score-based models.

title: Adaptive Scheduling Pipeline for Multi-Instance Asynchronous Reinforcement Learning
abstract: We present the Adaptive Scheduling Pipeline (ASP), an offline rollout scheduler for multi-instance asynchronous reinforcement learning (RL) of large language models (LLMs). ASP jointly reduces three sources of rollout underutilization - padding bubbles from intra-minibatch length heterogeneity, skewness bubbles from long-tail outputs, and sorting bubbles from fluctuations in training-queue occupancy induced by length-sorted dispatch - through a single offline preprocessing pass. This enables efficient multi-instance rollout that overcomes the early scaling plateau of single-instance inference while smoothing the arrival of generated samples at the trainer. We integrate the scheduler into an asynchronous architecture that decouples rollout from training while keeping policy lag observable and bounded. Complete ASP improves end-to-end throughput by up to 3.22 times and reduces iteration time by up to 76.8% relative to MindSpeed-RL, while reducing iteration time by up to 62.5% relative to verl. Within ASP, scheduling reduces mean iteration time by 10.9%. ASP also scales more robustly with additional generation resources than these baselines and shows no visible convergence degradation in the measured bounded-lag regime. ASP has since been used in an internal telecom-domain RL post-training workflow, reducing the reported training period from more than three months to about two months and producing a domain-enhanced model for knowledge answering and tool calling.

title: A lightweight convolutional neural network for target detection in an edge environment
abstract: This paper proposes a novel, lightweight convolutional neural network (CNN) designed for edge device deployment. The CNN is developed to recognize and classify threats or targets of interest. The model is equipped with a real-time hotspot detection algorithm, which enables it to process information quickly and accurately, resulting in improved inference time of up to 20 fps and a detection range of more than 400 meters with typical thermal situational awareness sensors. The proposed CNN has been rigorously tested and validated to demonstrate its high accuracy, sensitivity, and low false positive rate, providing a reliable solution for edge devices to detect potential targets. Additionally, the lightweight design of the CNN allows for easy deployment, making it an ideal solution for extending the security bubble for edge devices. The proposed model can be used for a variety of applications, including surveillance, security, and object recognition.

title: Align3D: Image-Structure Co-Aligned 3D Scene Generation with Observability-Aware Fidelity-Preserving Guidance
abstract: We present Align3D, an image-conditioned diffusion model that generates 3D indoor layouts that are both faithful to a single input photograph and physically plausible beyond the observed view. From the photograph we infer a confidence-calibrated scene graph and train a set-diffusion layout denoiser with image-structure co-alignment where confidence-weighted modality fusion balances image and scene-graph alignment using predicted confidences, while observability-aware fidelity-preserving guidance projects conflicting scene-quality gradients and reweighs them with an object-level confidence mask so under-observed degrees of freedom absorb physical priors without undoing the image-graph match. On 3D-FRONT, Align3D improves image-alignment and scene-quality metrics over recent baselines; once trained, it maps previously unseen photographs to layouts in a single feed-forward pass.

title: Do Intelligent Tutoring Systems Benefit K-12 Students? A Meta-Analysis and Evaluation of Heterogeneity of Treatment Effects in the U.S.
abstract: To expand the use of intelligent tutoring systems (ITS) in K-12 schools, it is essential to understand the conditions under which their use is most beneficial. This meta-analysis evaluated the heterogeneity of ITS effects across studies focusing on elementary, middle, and high schools in the U.S. It included 18 studies with 77 effect sizes across 11 ITS. Overall, there was a significant positive effect size of ITS on U.S. K-12 students' learning outcomes (g=0.271, SE=0.011, p=0.001). Furthermore, effect sizes were similar across elementary and middle schools, and for low-achieving students, but were lower in studies including rural schools. A MetaForest analysis showed that providing worked-out examples, intervention duration, intervention condition, type of learning outcome, and immediate measurement were the most important moderators of treatment effects.
